speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of utmost importance to Western Canada, that being the recent order in council of the federal government which will increase freight rates applicable to the movement of rapeseed products and which will in turn have the effect of curtailing one of Western Canada's most promising industries, namely, rapeseed processing. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith):
That the Ministry of Transport refrain from any such move until thorough consultation can take place between the affected parties in Western Canada and the question of rate structures can be examined in detail by the Standing Committee on Transportation of this House.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED APPROVAL OF USE OF FRENCH IN AIR-TO-GROUND COMMUNICATIONS IN QUEBEC-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion concerning a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering that French is one of the official languages of Canada, that it is even the primary language of work in Quebec, considering that French-speaking pilots request the authorization to use French in air-to-ground communications, at least within the limits of Quebec, and that it has been shown that the use of French can sometimes become an important security factor, as indicated in the statement by Arvida pilot Marcel Deschamps who could save his own life, that of a passenger and his aircraft thanks to the cooperation of the military air controller at CFB Bagotville and of the captain of military helicopter 08 who both agreed to speak French, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):
That the House unanimously approve the use of French in air communications over Quebec territory.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister said it was not a gift, but I remind him that it is a 100 per cent subsidy, so he can call it what he likes. My supplementary question refers back to the Liberal party's campaign promise in the 1974 general election in which it was asserted that a new Crown agency of some sort was to be established to take over existing CPR and CNR passenger services. I put this question to the minister: Does the government still intend to go ahead with this plan or does this announcement by him in an ad hoc way mean the government is planning to abandon that proposal or when it implements it will we buy back from CP the $30 million gift we are giving it?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: POSSIBILITY CROWN AGENCY WILL RUN RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really find it extraordinary that the Leader of the New Democratic Party has not seen in this announcement the simple continuation of what was clearly indicated in my policy statement to the House of Commons in January. This simply is an implementation, which was indicated at that time, of one phase of the over-all program. I indicated at that time that whereas initially we had thought in terms of a new corporation to operate the passenger service which might be a direct government Crown corporation, we had judged at that point in time that it might be better to have a company which was really formed by CN-CP, much like the telecommunications operation, rather than come in with our own. But we do believe one company has to be operating passenger rail service in this country in order to have efficient and good passenger service. We will fall back upon our own creature if that is required.
This $30 million is not a transfer of money but will be compensation for a specific cost outlay in passenger service. Again in the policy statement it was made clear that we believed it essential to move to a total compensation system in order to have a good rail passenger system. The alternative simply is that the railways have to find cash by taxing other goods or they run down their service. We

believe that if there is good rail passenger service in this country it must be paid for by the passengers or the taxpayers. It is as simple as that.

speechtext: The announcement yesterday indicated that we were progressively moving in relation to all rail areas in Canada where passenger service is justified. We propose to do that. speechtext: That certainly is not my belief. I would like to address a question to the Prime Minister in view of the fact that the Minister of Transport is not prepared to take any action. I should like to point out to the Prime minister that, since there are no longer any enforced controls on travel agents reporting ticket sales and, as of October, 1975, there were an excess of 96,000 unreported travel agent ticket sales, which represents a minimum of $2,208,000 unpaid for transportation, will the Prime Minister launch an immediate investigation and also give an assurance that the finance branch will not be moved to Montreal? Will he also check to see when the lease expires in the Richardson Building in Winnipeg?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF FINANCE BRANCH AT WINNIPEG AND ASSURANCE BRANCH NOT MOVED TO MONTREAL
speechtext: What building?

be trying to run one of its Crown corporations from the floor of the House of Commons. maintopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF FINANCE BRANCH AT WINNIPEG AND ASSURANCE BRANCH NOT MOVED TO MONTREAL

maintopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF FINANCE BRANCH AT WINNIPEG AND ASSURANCE BRANCH NOT MOVED TO MONTREAL
speechtext: Since when did you ask our position on anything?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF FINANCE BRANCH AT WINNIPEG AND ASSURANCE BRANCH NOT MOVED TO MONTREAL
speechtext: We are talking about public money and taxpayers' money, and I would like to point out to the Prime Minister that at the present time there are employees sitting in the offices doing nothing.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF FINANCE BRANCH AT WINNIPEG AND ASSURANCE BRANCH NOT MOVED TO MONTREAL
speechtext: Question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF FINANCE BRANCH AT WINNIPEG AND ASSURANCE BRANCH NOT MOVED TO MONTREAL
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member was permitted a rather strong representation as a preliminary to his second supplementary. In this question I wonder whether he would go directly to the question.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF FINANCE BRANCH AT WINNIPEG AND ASSURANCE BRANCH NOT MOVED TO MONTREAL
speechtext: Yes, I can go directly to the question. Air Canada is paying outside contractors $6 per hour to do ticket sorting while ticket sorters are sitting idle in the offices of the Winnipeg finance branch, and I think the Prime Minister is going to have to take some responsibility here to get this mess cleaned up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF FINANCE BRANCH AT WINNIPEG AND ASSURANCE BRANCH NOT MOVED TO MONTREAL
speechtext: The only responsibility I will take at this present time is the one which the Minister of Transport properly took in answering the question. We will refer the concerns of the hon. member to the Crown corporation and trust it to deal with them properly. If the Crown corporation does not deal with them properly, surely that will be brought to light by the report of the accountants who audit the books of the corporation. The hon. member shakes his head, but this is the principle of Crown corporations. They should not be managed on a day to day basis by the government, even upon representations in the House of Commons. For instance, frequently representations are made about the CBC. The hon. member, and certainly his party, would not like us to interfere with the management of the CBC, in spite of the representations they make. We refer these questions to the Crown corporations and trust that they will be dealt with fairly.

REQUEST FOR CONSULTATION WITH UNION REPRESENTATIVES CONCERNING DANGER OF CANCER CAUSED BY BLUE FIBRE ASBESTOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Has the government reached any decision regarding the banning of the import into Canada of blue fibre asbestos? I ask this question again in view of the

danger to workers of a fatal cancer caused by blue fibre asbestos. Will the minister undertake to consult, with respect to this danger and this request, with the unions representing workers at the Johns-Manville plant in Scarborough?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: REQUEST FOR CONSULTATION WITH UNION REPRESENTATIVES CONCERNING DANGER OF CANCER CAUSED BY BLUE FIBRE ASBESTOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a while ago the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and myself announced our intention to proceed to the banning of blue fibre asbestos. There have been consultations with the firm involved after it made further scientific representations. We have since examined those further scientific representations. We have come to the conclusion that those representations were not of such a nature as to change our original intention. My colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, intends to make an announcement shortly on this subject, and I think he should be the one to answer with regard to this particular aspect.
As far as the latter part of the question is concerned, I am pleased to receive the representation of the hon. member with regard to the unions concerned. I will instruct my officials to make themselves available to the union officials, at their convenience, and to make available to them the scientific information we have on this particular subject.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will make my statement as concisely as possible and I will read it as fast as possible. I mention that the volume of mail has increased tremendously in the last four years, from 4 billion to 5.5 billion pieces. Our surveys on service which have been taken weekly and monthly indicate that the level of service now being acheived by the Post Office is more and more acceptable to the Canadian people.
I draw attention to postal rates in other countries and to the fact that we have not increased our rates for four years. The United States is now charging a basic first-class rate of 13 cents, the United Kingdom 17 cents, France 18 cents, and Australia 23 cents. During this period of four years, costs have risen for such things as labour, fuel, transportation, buildings and machinery. The gap between the cost of

May 21, 1976
Change in Postal Rates
the service and the charge to our customers has continually widened.
More particularly, Post Office customers-and it may be of interest that 80 per cent of our mail is generated by 20 per cent of the users-have been asking us when we intend to increase our rates so that they can undertake their own planning for the future. We intend to introduce changes to the Post Office Act to deal with this whole question and our relationship with industry. Furthermore, in the interim we should like to introduce certain measures now in order to give as much notice as possible of how the Post Office is planning ahead. For this reason, using the authority under the Financial Administration Act, I intend to introduce an interim change in the basic first-class postal rates on September 1, 1976, from 8 cents to 10 cents, and a further increase in this rate on March 1, 1977, from 10 cents to 12 cents.
Canada Post Office recognizes that many of our customers were adversely affected by the recent postal disruptions. Consequently, some of the rate changes in other classes of mail will be graduated both to cushion the effect of the strike and to allow for longer range planning. As a result of strong representations made to me by my colleagues, in particular by the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) who is concerned for the welfare of the Canadian publishing industry, a 20 per cent increase in second-class mail rates will not take effect until March 1, 1977. I might point out that this is 20 per cent of the basic rate of five cents, so I am talking about a copper.
Changes in rates for other classes of mail, including the important third-class direct mail category, will go into effect on dates which are still under discussion with the appropriate parties. That is the association representing the bulk mail industry. The Post Office is planning a complete review of its rate structure in that category with the view to a more realistic determination of postal charges for the services rendered. There are some association which are currently using third-class mail for their publications, and these may warrant some form of government support or subsidy. I propose to review this question with my colleagues with the view to having certain departments assume the cost of any assistance which may be identified as a result of this review.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to agree immediately with the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) that there were some negotiations as to how we should handle the announcement that he has just made. When we moved into committee of supply yesterday there were discussions as to how we should proceed. We have got a little out of practise with the proper procedure in this regard.
When Your Honour indicated there were some precedents for making a statement of this kind on an opposition day, which today is going to be primarily concerned with Post Office affairs, I could see immediately that we were heading into some procedural difficulties. Now that the Postmaster General has made a statement, I will respond briefly and reserve my more detailed comments until we move into committee of the whole. The Postmaster General has chosen a rather unfortunate day to lead with his chin 
in this respect. He is an Irishman, and the Irish have a habit of doing things of this kind. There is another quality of the Irish which I think might be referred to at this juncture: they have the optimism of Finian in Finian's Rainbow.
Someone suggested, when we were discussing the announcement the Postmaster General was to make, that obviously the increased rates must be for the payment of the extended storage period required because of the continuing delay in the delivery of Canada's mail. My immediate response is to suggest to the Postmaster General that there is no evidence of restraint here. He must be having difficulty reconciling his role as Postmaster General in this respect with his new responsibility as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
The proposed rate increase exceeds the Anti-Inflation Board guidelines and regulations. I suppose it is designed to overcome the growing deficit which has been increasing rather substantially with each passing year with the current deficit for the 1976-77 period estimated at some $630 million. Hon. members must agree that it requires a combination of sharply rising costs, mismanagement and inefficiency to run up a deficit of that size. That is a fair appraisal of the situation. The Postmaster General has frequently said there is a malaise, a sickness in the Post Office Department. We intend to suggest, during the course of the debate today, that this sickness or malaise still persists notwithstanding the optimistic note of the Postmaster General's statement this morning.
The statement was placed in an unfortunate context. The opening statement was to the effect that the Postmaster General restrained himself in announcing any increase in postal rates until the Post Office had achieved a satisfactory level of efficiency. In spite of reassuring statistics from postal officials about on-time delivery and efficiency, the public seems increasingly convinced that postal service has gone from bad to worse. I spend a good deal of my time, as Post Office critic, dealing with complaints which come in from all parts of Canada in respect of continuing problems of the Post Office Department. This will be substantiated by contributions my colleagues will make during the debate today. There is a steady stream of complaints. Everybody has heard stories of damaged, lost, stolen and delayed mail, sometimes with horrendous consequences. I am not sure I should move into this phase at the moment. Perhaps I could delay it until the study of the estimates in committee of the whole. I have a series of quotations from government departments, some as recent as March 15, which indicates they are less than happy with the Post Office Department. This has specific reference to the use of courier service. Let us have a look at the Privy Council Office complaints.

I will save that for later and conclude my remarks by indicating that the increase has been justified in part by a reference to increases which have been announced over recent years in the United States and the United Kingdom. That also was an unfortunate context in which to place the statement, because customers in the United States are curtailing their use of the mails and turning to alternate services. As the rates go up, public resistance grows more firm and volumes drop even more, creating a vicious circle. In fact, I would suggest that the postal service is making the same mistake the railroads made, and in light of the discussions that took place in this House earlier today we realize the consequences of that decision to Canada. Obviously, when rates go up exorbitantly without a corresponding increase in efficiency of service, the Canadian public, particularly the business community which is the large user of postal services, will turn to cheaper and more efficient modes of communication.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I received two statements this morning in which there was a slight change. In part of the first paragraph of the first statement it is stated:
-recent surveys which indicate that the level of productivity achieved by the Post Office is becoming more and more acceptable to the Canadian people.
This was changed in the revised version as follows:
Recent surveys indicate that the level of service achieved by the Post Office is becoming more and more acceptable to the Canadian people.
That was a very necessary change because, obviously, productivity is not one of the great achievements of the Post Office Department, as we shall demonstrate during the discussion that takes place today. It is very important that we have this discussion today, and I will not prolong its commencement further at this stage.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the debate on the Post Office estimates I will be very brief in my remarks regarding the minister's announcement. It seems strange to me that a government committed to fighting inflation should propose a 50 per cent increase in the cost of first-class mail service by March of next year. It is doubly strange to me that this proposal is made by the Postmaster General who is also the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, because in that role he should be interested in knowing what this sharp increase will mean in the cost of living of every individual who uses the mail to send letters to friends and relatives, and every company that uses first-class mail for billing and other forms of business communication. They will all be affected by this sharp increase. In the case of the business community, this increase will be passed on to the consumer in the form of higher prices.
The NDP does not accept the principle that each part of the postal service must be self-sustaining or, indeed, that postal services must pay their way.

vices, which of necessity must be run with a deficit. We do not believe personal letters written to families and friends by individual citizens should necessarily cover the full cost of delivery. We believe that the reading of newspapers and magazines is so important to Canadians and the Canadian identity that the cost of this delivery service should be subsidized by the Canadian people as a whole.
In the same way, we question the good sense of increasing the cost of first-class mail at this time and it being done alone. We certainly object to the postponement of decisions in respect of the increase concerning third-class mail charges particularly when we realize that so much of the unsolicited mail-what is commonly referred to as junk mail-is moved and paid for as third-class mail. The latest figures I have for last indicate that there was a deficit of $130 million for third-class mail. It seems to us that the minister would have been much better advised to have sharply increased the rate for third-class mail, particularly junk mail before he increased the cost of first-class mail. We certainly object to that step being taken at this time.

According to his statement, the purpose of the increase would be to reduce the deficit of the Canadian post office which, if I am not mistaken, amounted to some $500 million last year. I appreciate that the minister is right in believing that this increase is justified and that in advocating it he is only doing what is expected of him, just like a good soldier obeys his superiors. The only difference between him and a good soldier, as far as obeying orders is concerned, is that the minister receives his instructions from high financial circles and complies with a system which urges him to act the way he does, namely increase the postage.
In his statement, the minister said he was trying to make up for the deficit which was incurred last year. But do you really think that this will solve all the problems? I do not think so. It may help for a while but eventually the same situation will arise, perhaps within a few years. And that is because the system is inadequate and cannot meet the needs and expectations of the Canadian people.
For many years we, the Social Credit Party of Canada, have tried with every means available to us to make the government understand that all the economic problems we are facing proceed from our financial system. If the financial system were consistent with reality, there would be no inflation, not to mention deflation, nor any price increases.
We are sure, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians would see a gradual price decline as progress would show up in techniques and production processes. What we want most of all is that the government change its goals and its legislation implementation in order that they become fair for all Canadians, and thus the situation would improve. But as long as the government will not implement what we have tried for many years to make them understand, the same

May 21, 1976
Order Paper Questions
situation will prevail and we will sink ever deeper into the economic depression we are now facing.
We believe that the situation will improve if production is pushed up. To this end we have to work harder and harder, because we are a rich country, we have natural resources, we have large quantities of raw materials, and enough manpower. What else can we ask for? Yet we are faced in Canada with an unemployment rate of 9 per cent. There are people, and they are numerous, who cannot make both ends meet, and to cap it all a new increase has just been announced today.
At the present time, Mr. Speaker, we are mere slaves of finance and corporations, of this government. I think that should the government ever respect and protect the human being instead of finance, as is presently the case, inflation will have disappeared and it will be more pleasant to live, because there will be fewer thefts, less drugs, fewer murders, and certainly more mutual aid and understanding.
I am aware that the postal strike of last fall has underlined the problem of relations between wages and prices, and that the deficit which we experienced last year and which we will probably experience again this year, if it does not grow larger, will depend partly upon that and upon inflation in general, because, faced with a constantly increasing cost of living, and also to take advantage of the material and economic progress achieved each year and each day in our country, something must be done.

Post Office
Resolved, that a sum not exceeding $977,488,000 be granted to Her Majesty for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1977 (less the amount voted in interim supply) as follows: Vote 1-Operation expenditures, contributions and authorizations to spend receipts of the year for financial services and others-$977,488,000.

Mr. Chairman, now we can get on with the business at hand for the day, after our little diversion. I trust that during the course of the day we will have the opportunity to deal with questions and answers in the committee which will raise specific issues that are concerning members of parliament from their various constituencies.
I am very happy to see the Postmaster General in his place, because I think the consideration of estimates in committee of the whole is one of the great losses to our parliamentary system. There was a time when we used to practice the basic principle of parliamentary democracy- no taxation without representation. The minister used to sit on the griddle until all the queries, questions and grievances had been dealt with, and only then was he allowed to proceed with his estimates. We are very circumscribed in the time allocation today, but at least we will have a chance to deal with specific problems.
The preamble to the estimates states that the basic function of Canada's Post Office Department is to provide postal services to the people of Canada at reasonable rates and a standard of service adequate to meet their needs without incurring subsidization from general taxation. I think we will discover today that the Post Office Department at present is meeting few, if any, of the exalted goals outlined in that statement. As we already indicated in the preliminary discussion, rates are increasing, complaints from the public are increasing, the deficit is increasing, and unfortunately the great principle that was first enunciated by the pioneers of the postal service, that it is the indispensable chain that binds the nation together, no longer has any validity.
I could go into some of the recent history of the decline of the Post Office but I will not take the time on this occasion to do that. The decision was made a few years ago to change the Post Office Department into a business with managerial expertise, to the neglect of public service and consumer and labour relations. I know the Postmaster General during his incumbency in the Post Office Department has been trying to overcome the errors that were made a few years ago, but obviously he has not been successful and he now takes the easier route of increasing postal rates in order to cover up the problems and the
Business of Supply
deficiencies of the postal service which have largely contributed to the increase in the Post Office deficit.
We need recite the fact of 24 illegal strikes in five years until 1975 to indicate where the labour relations situation stands. We can refer, and we will refer, to the marketing gimmicks that have come in rapid succession-very expensive ones-which have not dealt with the basic malaise of the Post Office Department. Indeed, many of these marketing gimmicks have led to more and more of the business fleeing to the private couriers. I wish to refer to the unhappiness as expressed by some replies to a question on the use of the courier services by government departments on March 15. Here is what the Unemployment Insurance Commission has to say. It expends some $375,000 annually in private courier service. It says:
The Post Office Department cannot provide overnight delivery between the regional offices and the district offices . .. We must use private couriers to supplement existing Post Office services.
So much for the assured mail delivery program which came out a few years ago guaranteeing overnight service within particular areas. The Privy Council Office has something similar to say, "We require, urgently, prompt services outside Ottawa-Hull within 24 hours, and this cannot be guaranteed by the Post Office Department. Letters, documents or small packages which must reach their destination within a time limit which cannot be guaranteed by the Post Office Department, we send through courier route. Regular mail services were not used because they were not available, or couriers were faster and more economical. In addition, the Post Office could not give an assurance that mail could be delivered within the time limit required."
The statement made by the minister today indicates that the volume of mail has increased. I want to pose as my first question the following: How much of this is dependent upon the promotional work of the Post Office Department for Olympic stamps and coins? I get constant complaints, as I am sure do other hon. members, that the Post Office Department is contacting almost every householder in Canada with a slick package, urging them to buy either Olympic coins or Olympic stamps and I think the postage alone for this mailing is 20 cents plus the return mail. A more recent venture in this regard is the use of the telepost which is the new marketing facility which is supposed to speed up urgent business communications in Canada. In a telepost message that went out from the minister's office to, I presume, hundreds of thousands of people across Canada urging them to subscribe, we read the following words:
As a previous patron of Canada's stamp sculpture program, you were personally informed by Mr. Mackasey of the introduction of series IV stamp sculptures. All orders addressed to Mr. Mackasey's office at the House of Commons will receive priority treatment. Olympic stamp sculptures are unique commemorative works of art and valuable items for serious collectors and investors. Minting and delivery time now just two weeks. Orders must be postmarked by deadline of May 15.
I believe a message like that costs about 75 cents each, which would account for a lot of the upsurge in Post Office business and revenue to which the minister referred in his report. One of the weaknesses of the Post Office Department has been its failure in public relations. I raised an issue in the question period some weeks ago with respect to this situation concerning the use of third class mail by
95568 -37V2

May 21, 1976
Business of Supply
the Kinsmen Rehabilitation Foundation of British Columbia. They went into considerable detail in outlining the complaint. The only action that was achieved as a result of that complaint was that the public relations people came along and said that obviously the Kinsmen had not packaged the material properly, and if they had there would have been a greater response to the appeal on behalf of the disabled people of British Columbia.
Furthermore, there is a low return on the basis of this sort of mailing. The point that the foundation was making was that they did not want a public relations exercise; they wanted a customer relations exercise which would deal specifically with the complaint, because they were contemplating sending out 400,000 mailings if there could be an assurance and a guarantee that the mailing would reach the people concerned. So I raise that issue once again with the Postmaster General. It is not public relations which is wanted; it is good customer relations.
Administration of the Post Office Department is constantly under criticism, mainly because of the increase in managerial staff as compared with service and delivery staff. Executive, scientific and professional categories have tripled from 43 in recent years to the present number of 127. In eight years over-all employment in the Post Office Department has increased fron 39,180 to 60,524, but the large percentage increase has been in the executive, scientific and professional categories. This is a complaint which comes from the letter carriers and the postal workers who are the people who really provide the service directly to the public.
There is another inquiry I would like the Postmaster General to consider. The marketing branch has been active. There has been a new marketing manager appointed who is supposed to have expertise in this regard. Publications such as the communication publication, and now the new customer publication, have obviously taken a good part of the Post Office budget. In spite of this marketing and customer relations, customer complaints increased by 16.3 per cent between 1970 and 1975, and indemnities due to loss of mail have increased by substantial percentages.
The private courier matter has already been dealt with in the House, and in response to a question I asked recently the Postmaster General indicated that the Post Office is intending to go back into the courier business, which now takes about $70 million in revenue from the Post Office Department. The Postmaster General said he is aware that when they cream off the business, they are costing the taxpayer, and that his department is going to make a pitch for all of it. Well, that is a mixed blessing because obviously people are using the private couriers because they are providing people more efficient service than the Post Office. This is why so many government departments have moved in this direction. The Postmaster General and his officials will have to see to it that they can restore the confidence of the public if they are going to move back into this market. The experience in the United States is that with their increasing costs of postal delivery and their deficit, running at $1.5 billion currently, the post office department there is losing more and more of the business to competitors. Certainly an increase in rates without a corresponding increase in efficiency in Canada will not

deal with the problem which was outlined in the minister's statement this morning.
Basic to the back of efficient services of the Post Office Department is the low morale of the employees. The strike situation points that cut, and we are hoping that there will be a happier relationship. I want to bring a few points to the attention of the minister. There is still indifference toward the human needs of the postal employees following the settlement of the contracts of last year. People are more important than machines, and I continually get the complaint that the employees at the managerial level keep talking about plugging the people into the automated system. The coder-sorter issue is still not resolved. For example, in the Vancouver post office, even though the assistant deputy minister says that the coding category must be changed to coder, sweeper and sorter, coders are still only coding. This was one of the big issues in the automation battle. The Taylor report is clear in this regard, and it was obvious that the plant managers are defying even the wishes of an assistant deputy minister at the level of Mr. Gordon Sinclair.
Consultation, which is important to human relations, is restricted to issuing an order. The National Film Board has been travelling from post office to post office doing a film on labour relations, and I imagine this will become available to the Postmaster General. I am sure he will find the comments of the employees informative in this regard.
The letter carriers raise the issue of the failure of the Post Office Department to provide house-to-house delivery to an increasing number of communities across the country. One of my colleagues will be dealing with this. This is the negative kind of restraint which does serious damage to the reputation of the Post Office Department because it fails to provide the basic services which are required.
The association of postal employees, which is in the bargaining process now, has reached an impasse. We discussed this in the House of Commons recently. They are faced with a situation where supervisors in certain categories are going to receive less income than the personnel they supervise. It has not been resolved in some categories. Now that the negotiations have reached the crucial stage it is impossible to bring the Post Office representatives back to the bargaining table because they cannot get a mandate from Treasury Board. I submit to the Postmaster General that the reason his officials are hesitating to come back to the bargaining table is that they have such a miserable offer to make, and the situation is going to be further aggravated because on July 1 there is to be a further 6 per cent increase, under the existing terms of the contract, to postal employees. The minister is aware of this.
He talks about industrial democracy. Industrial democracy requires real consultation where, as the minister himself has said, supervisors will no longer tell employees what to do and how to do it. The supervisors will ask the workers how they think it should be done, and restoring dignity and prestige of the postal employees is a huge job calling for adjustment at every level of management. As we approach the hour of adjournment, I remind the Postmaster General of those words and hope that he will be able to get real industrial democracy working in the Post Office Department. Perhaps the military posture of the Post Office is too deeply ingrained. There are still postmas-
May 21, 1976

ters around who expect their workers to come to attention in their presence. I am sure the hon. gentleman agrees that this is not conducive to good human relations. The very term "Postmaster General" has military overtones, and I trust that in his actual contacts with the employees he will not aggravate that image by the posture he assumes.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, we had an opportunity today to discuss the problems of the Post Office-the delivery of mail, which is considered by many people to be unsatisfactory, the large deficit the department has experienced in recent years and will undoubtedly face in the coming year, and the announcement by the minister this morning that in an effort to reduce the size of the deficit he proposes to increase the cost of first-class mail by some 50 per cent in the next year.
Undoubtedly, part of the reason for the problems in the Post Office can be found in the very bad relationships that exist between senior officials in the department and the employees. Because I do not want to be accused of being partisan-which I am, and which I admit-let me put on the record a description of the situation in the Post Office given by none other than the Postmaster General in a letter which appeared in the Globe and Mail on April 25, 1975. I shall only read part of the letter, Mr. Chairman, but I think it describes the situation much more eloquently than I could ever hope to. In that letter the Postmaster General said:
One can make a strong case that the workers are extremely militant-that their productivity leaves much to be desired; that they have continuously taken the law into their own hands, and, on some occasions resorted to violence.
In the year or more since that letter was written the Postmaster General has told this House frequently-in fact, I would say ad nauseam-how true that statement is. The letter continues:
But one can make an equally strong case that the employer, that is, the government, over a long period of time, has been anything but a model employer. As a member of government, I accept my share of responsibility and single out no individual as more responsible or less responsible for this fact.
Inadequate compensation, work places that are a disgrace, uneven managerial policy, regimentation that at times has bordered on a military mentality, has, over the years, resulted in a slow but steady reduction in morale, in pride of association and in inevitable hostility on the part of the workers.
Later in the letter he said:
As a government, we have an obligation to be at least as good an employer as the more enlightened employers in the private sector. I believe that this is now well understood-both among my colleagues, and, perhaps more important in this bureaucratic jungle, understood by the bureaucrats.
Business of Supply
When the hon. member for Brandon-Souris was speaking, one of my Social Credit colleagues said, "I have heard all these things before". That is true, unfortunately. We have to make essentially the same speeches because the more the minister speaks, the less things change. I turned up some old files, Mr. Chairman, and found an article published in the Montreal Gazette in 1974, written by George Radwanski, in which he summarized a report made in 1966 by Mr. Justice Montpetit who had investigated the situation in the Post Office. I should like to quote a couple of paragraphs of the report of Mr. Justice Montpetit:
A large number of the Post Office employees' grievances are, first and foremost, human relations problems.
Except in one or two districts, the attitude of some supervisors and postmasters toward their employees leaves much to be desired. These people have only a vague notion of the importance of maintaining good relations with their staff . ..
A well conceived policy of consultation and of exchange of viewpoints at all levels becomes essential. The dialogue must not become a mere formality to which one has to submit and which is considered more or less a waste of time or mere idle chatter. Nor must it become a one-sided conversation.
Nothing has changed since Mr. Justice Montpetit made that report. The minister may say that things have changed. The Letter Carriers' Union, which had a much better relationship with the minister and the department than the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, commissioned a study some years later by Professor Vanderberg, a professor of economics at Carleton University. He found:
-still inadequate consultation at the root of postal employees' grievances.
Harmonious industrial relations cannot be achieved without a meaningful airing of views.
The initiative for the inauguration of such discussion on any topic logically rests with the party which is considering the implementation of a new policy.
It is the Post Office which decided to make major technological changes. It decided to automate the sorting of mail and everything else. No one in this party ever questioned, nor do we question now, the necessity of using the most modern methods for sorting and delivering mail. We recognize that sorting mail by hand would make it prohibitive, cost-wise. We realize that without using the latest techniques the mail service would be slowed to such an extent that people would no longer use it.
I do not believe that the postal workers, certainly never publicly, or their union officials have ever opposed automation. However, they have a very legitimate concern. Automation should not be brought in at their expense. Masses of workers should not be laid off. If money is saved through the use of automatic equipment, the workers should get part of the benefits. From that point of view they are no different from workers in private industry.
In the Post Office we have continual objection and guerilla warfare against these feelings of the workers. Let me illustrate very briefly. When the sorting equipment was brought in, the rate of pay for the sorters was set much lower than the rate for hand sorting. You do not have to be an expert in work procedure to know that watching an automatic sorter handling thousands of letters a minute is a lot more difficult than sorting by hand. However, the Post Office, Treasury Board or whoever

May 21, 1976
Business of Supply
makes these decisions, insisted on this. It took months of threats and strikes before the Post Office agreed to at least pay the same amount per hour to those manning the automatic sorting machines.
Professor Vanderberg and Mr. Justice Montpetit talked about consultation. The postal workers were worried about the effects of automation on their employment, and there was a bitter strike. In the new collective agreement in which this minister was involved there is a clause to the effect that there shall be discussion and agreement with regard to any new automatic equipment being brought in. Did that happen? No. Last week the union tried to take the Post Office to court, claiming that a new post office had been begun in New Brunswick without the role of the workers being worked out in advance.
That was in Newfoundland.

Newfoundland, I am sorry. The case was dismissed by the court. I do not say the workers were right in that or any other case. However, if the workers felt so strongly about not being consulted that they went to court, the bargaining process has in fact broken down. I say that even if the workers were wrong, because this should have been settled before it was necessary to go to court. I am sure there are still hundreds of thousands, and I say this advisedly, of grievance cases filed by the union. Why? Because nothing is ever settled voluntarily by the Post Office.
I know we are dealing with a union which has a reputation for being very militant. It is not the easiest thing in the world to settle disputes with a militant union, but it takes two to tango, it takes two to have a fight. I am not convinced, by anything I have seen since coming to parliament, that those occupying the senior positions in the Post Office Department do not want to fight. Why are there so many grievances? I am told that if the department loses at a relatively low stage of grievance procedure, it appeals to the ajudicator. If the decision of the adjudicator is not to the liking of the department, they take the case to court. That means delays of months or years. It costs the unions thousands of dollars. That is not the way to get co-operation and to boost morale. In addition, I am told that if a decision at any level is in favour of the position taken by the union, the Post Office Department takes the position that all that has been settled is one particular case. If there are 50 other cases of a similar nature, the union must fight each one individually.
This situation has gone on for a long time. I remember making the same kind of appeal to a former postmaster general, Mr. Kierans. I suggested to him that the almost military organization and discipline which the present Postmaster General spoke of in the letter from which I quoted no longer meets the needs of the country or the Post Office. That condition has existed since the Post Office began. I suggest it is time to get rid of that system.
If it is necessary, in order to get rid of that system, to begin by getting rid of most of those who occupy the top positions in the Post Office itself, particularly those involved in labour-management, this is what ought to be done. I made that suggestion six or seven years ago, and I
[Mr. Orlikow.)
make it again to the present minister. I say to the hon. gentleman publicly what I say to him privately-that I have a great deal of respect for him. He has demonstrated on more than one occasion that he is a friend of working people. I would have expected that he would at least have begun the job of changing the situation in the top levels of the Post Office Department, so that we could hope to see an improvement in the relationship between the unions and the department as well as between the employees and the department.
I am confident that regardless of the tens of millions of dollars we are spending on automating and renovating the system, we shall not benefit from an efficient postal delivery system until we have created a situation in which the employees are happy, proud of working for the Post Office and prepared to do a fair day's work in return for a fair day's pay. I believe they are getting a fair day's pay and I want them to do a fair day's work. I believe they will do so when they get human and decent consideration from the people who direct the work of the department.
The minister has had a difficult year. He has been through some bruising battles with the postal workers and their unions, and I want to say to him, as I have said elsewhere, that there were faults on both sides. I hope both sides can forget what has happened in the past and use their efforts to change the situation in such a way as to provide the kind of postal service of which people can be proud. I hope the minister will give the kind of leadership which most of us expect him to give, although I must say I have seen little sign of it so far.

Mr. Chairman, I want to spend my time this afternoon by addressing a few questions to the minister in the hope of eliciting some information on a few matters which are of great interest to the Canadian public. The first aspect I should like to explore relates to a question I asked in the House a year or so ago: whether the minister and his officials had taken steps to upgrade studies which had been carried out under an earlier regime into the possibility of placing the services presently carried out by the Post Office Department under the direction of a Crown corporation. Has the hon. gentleman investigated this possibility and weighed the advantages, or disadvantages, of following such a course?
At the time I asked my question, the minister suggested I should read an article in Time magazine showing that the United States post office had experienced huge deficits after following that route and placing its post office under the control of an independent agency. Recently, too, we have read about the difficulties the United Kingdom is experiencing in this regard. Nevertheless, the fact that there have been problems in other countries ought not, in my view, to prevent us looking at the Canadian scene and asking ourselves whether a change should not be considered here.
In this connection, I would refer to the comments made by the previous speaker on the subject of the relationship between management and unions in the Post Office Department. It seems to me that if the whole organization were brought under the roof of a Crown corporation, certain advantages would follow-advantages of the kind enjoyed, for example, by Ontario Hydro and other public utilities. Management and staff could get together to iron
May 21, 1976

out their problems without being involved, for example, with the Public Service Commission, as is the case with the Post Office.
There would be other benefits. The corporation would be able to plan and build its own buildings, put in the facilities needed, without having to turn to another department of government. The analogy that occurs to me is that of the distribution of electricity in my own province of Ontario. I think it is accepted that had this service been left in the early days of the century to a department of the provincial government, our lights would still be flickering. Instead, the responsibility was handed over to a Crown corporation, and I believe most people would say that it has been handled in a most efficient manner. Management has, over the years, tended to be extremely good. Perhaps the minister would comment on this aspect.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I did forgo my right to make a formal speech at the opening of the debate in deference to hon. members who might wish to ask questions. I realize that this is a short day. I hope to express my philosophy in more general terms when I have an opportunity to wind up the debate later.
The idea of a Crown corporation has many attractions, and the hon. member has touched on some of them. My own thinking, as Postmaster General for several years, is that the efficiency of the Post Office could be improved somewhat if the Post Office were treated not exactly as a Crown corporation in the sense that Air Canada is a Crown corporation, but if it were brought in under another schedule, like the Mint, for example. Let me explain why I say this. In a moment of frustration two years ago I said the only role I had in opening a post office was to cut the ribbon-and I did not even get to choose the colour the ribbon would be. Post offices are built, and priorities determined, by the Department of Public Works. Machinery and equipment is bought by the Department of Supply and Services. Hiring and firing is done by the Public Service Commission.
A good part of my time is spent consulting with other departments and doing things we could do with much greater efficiency were the Post Office given a special status. That need not necessarily be a Crown corporation. I could explain the reasons for my reluctance to go all the way and to set up a Crown corporation, but this would take too much time. It is perhaps related to costs and to the unhappy situation in the United States where the post office is very close to a Crown corporation but still subject to a lot of political interference in regard to establishing rates and things of that nature.
So if I may sum up my reply to the hon. member for Scarborough West, yes, I think there should be special status for the Post Office in relation to the government and to other government departments, preferably along the lines of other organizations that come under government control, but with more of a "hands off" type of approach than is now the case. Thus, the Post Office would have a greater degree of autonomy in determining the day to day operation of the Post Office without having to solicit, enjoin, seduce, coerce, or call it what you will, other departments in order to obtain what we sometimes think
Business of Supply
should be priority items for the Post Office but other departments do not.
The approach of a Crown corporation is appealing and deceptively so. Perhaps it is a little too simplistic. I think a happy medium could be found between the present status of the Post Office as a department of government and a full time Crown corporation. There are dozens of these, and I could name them all; indeed, there are a number of schedules. I think that the Post Office sooner or later-and preferably sooner than later-should be put under another schedule.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Churchill.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, my understanding in discussions with the Chair earlier was that it was appropriate for members to take their 20 minutes and use them by asking the minister questions if they so wished. That is the process that I was following and I had not consumed more than 50 per cent of my time.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That is my understanding also. The hon. member for Scarborough West.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I am very much encouraged by the comments of the Postmaster General in this connection. The suggestion of establishing a Crown corporation was really an expression of hope that the Post Office would move away from being a direct government department. I think the Canadian public in general would very much endorse the kind of proposal that the Postmaster General has put forward this afternoon. If we stop short of making the Post Office Department a full Crown corporation, it should at least be able to operate entirely on its own, in essence unfettered by having to go to various other government departments simply to stay in business and to render an efficient service to the people in a very basic area.
The next point that I want to make relates to the statement made by the minister a little earlier this afternoon. The Canadian public is going to be asked-indeed, it is going to be told-to face a 25 per cent increase in first-class mail rates as of September 1, followed by a further 20 per cent increase as of March 1 next year. The combination of these two increases represents a 50 per cent increase over the rates that will be in effect on August 31 of this year.
I think I understand the argument that the Post Office does indeed lose money, that therefore any increase in the rates, so long as it does not produce a profit for the Post Office, can be justified even under the guidelines of the Anti-Inflation Board. In other words, no new profit is being generated because there was never a profit in the first place, and there will still be no profit.
However, Mr. Chairman, what I find difficult to accept- and I think the people in my constituency and across the country will find difficult to accept-is the imposition by the government of very substantial increases in a service which in this particular case is, I think we must accept, certainly not quite up to scratch at the present time, for whatever reason. I say for whatever reason; they may be many and varied. Nevertheless, the fact remains this is a service the government is offering the people of Canada

May 21, 1976
Business of Supply
which simply is not up to the degree of efficiency which I think the public is entitled to expect and receive.
In effect, the Post Office is saying, "Look, we are doing our best, but we are going to have to increase our rates by 25 per cent". No company in business today is allowed an increase of that amount, and I think quite properly so under the anti-inflation guidelines. Nevertheless, the government is doing so in one particular service area. It then will compound the situation six months later by throwing at the public another 20 per cent increase.
I am sure that the Postmaster General can establish, on straight economic grounds, that indeed the Post Office is not making a profit, and that therefore we should endeavour to cut back on government expenditures that would otherwise have to be provided to finance a larger deficit. But I think we need a clearcut explanation, which we as members of parliament can take back to our constituents, of the kind of matters mentioned earlier by the Postmaster General. We should indeed examine the idea of making the Post Office a separate organization outside of government. We must do all we can to increase the degree of efficiency. It is also important that the public be persuaded somehow or other to accept this at a time when they are asked to pay more for the service.
We know that many businesses today who can afford to do so are saying no thank you to the services offered by the government's Post Office. Instead they are employing a private service. The growth of private mail couriers has been fantastic over the past few years. But the problem is that private mail services are really only available to those who can afford them, such as medium-sized and large businesses. There is no question that they are more expensive. Nevertheless, there comes a point in the business world where you have to be assured that your mail is going to arrive at its destination and that you do receive the mail that is dispatched to you, because money is involved, the basic foundation of all business.
However, individual members of the public cannot afford to switch. They must put on their 10-cent or 12-cent stamp, as the case may be, and depend on the government service to deliver their letters to the places they are supposed to go. Increasingly I am being asked whether this service is being properly performed.
I wonder whether, Mr. Chairman, I can combine my two points in a question to the minister. Would the minister in some way or other assure the Canadian public, through this House, that everything will continue to be done to improve those areas of postal service today that are still lacking? Will he continue to search out the areas of real weakness, and do so prior to the first of the new increases coming into vogue?
In addition, he might look into the matter of the private couriers, determine how much business they are skimming away, and see if there is any way in which people using the private couriers can be encouraged to return to the government service. There are two ways of cutting costs. If we get more business, which means more revenue, since a lot of our expenses are fixed the net deficit of the Post Office will be reduced. I am concerned at the falling off of business at the present time, and the signs are it is increasingly falling off. This will further hamper the ability of the

Post Office to break even or to limit its losses to a reasonable amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in order to keep my answer short, I should inform the hon. gentleman that I covered a lot of these points in my general remarks this morning, particularly the point in respect of percentages. Perhaps I am kind of conditioned to percentages from my years as minister of labour. Someone the other day said he had doubled his daughter's weekly allowance. It went up 100 per cent, from 25 cents to 50 cents.
So percentages are meaningful only if they are tied to a base period, and this is one of the weaknesses of statistics. It is one thing to say that we have increased the cost of a stamp to the average Canadian by 25 per cent. It is equally true to say that since the average Canadian writes four letters a year, with this increase of two cents it will mean an increase in cost to the average citizen of eight cents a year. Assuming that we are wrong in that regard, it would mean an increase, on the average, of only 15 cents a year to the individual considering that Canadians do not write many letters, and 80 per cent of our volume comes from 20 per cent of our business community, I do not think this will have a detrimental effect in so far as inflation is concerned. I will talk about the effect on the business community a little later.
The hon. gentleman made an extremely valid point, and perhaps it accentuates exactly what I am saying. As I mentioned earlier today, even with our proposed increases, which are phased in over almost a year, ours is still the cheapest or most inexpensive first-class mail service in the world.
And the slowest.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
Let us take the extreme. When we do reach the 12-cent cost, compared with the cost of first-class mail in West Germany and in other countries, which is now over 20 cents and in some cases 25 cents, with penalties for odd-shaped envelopes, and the rest of it, I do not think our service costs very much. The hon. gentleman also referred to courier service and I intend to refer to that in depth in my speech. He made it quite clear that people are quite prepared to pay substantial sums of money for courier service if they can get assured mail delivery. This is really what people are looking for. I am not as concerned about the increase, which is nominal, but rather about whether the people are going to get the service.
It might be of interest to the hon. gentleman and to other members of the House to know that most private carriers did not operate nationally during the strike. They did not make a great deal of money not because they were overloaded. They had no facilities from Toronto to Montreal, from Toronto to North Bay or to Vancouver. The reason they did not have the facilities is that they use the Canadian Post Office.

Mr. Chairman, it gives me pleasure to be able to speak on the Post Office estimates today. I should like to confine my remarks to northern mail service in our country. Many years ago, but as recently as 1950, people in the north were receiving their mail by a man on
May 21, 1976

snowshoes, carrying a pack. They then advanced to the use of dog teams. At least at that time they knew they were going to get mail once a year. That is not the situation now in at least three post offices in northern Manitoba, namely, Poplar River, Garden Hill and Wasagamack. This increase in the postal rates really does not affect the people in those communities. They could not care if it was 50 cents a letter because at the present time they do not have postal service at all in their communities.
Let me first speak of the community of Garden Hill. You may think this is a small community of 150 people, but there are 1,200 people living in Garden Hill. Their family allowances, their hydro bills and their old age pension cheques come in by mail. On April 1, 1976, an auditor arrived from the Post Office Department. According to the rules, I suppose an auditor can check the books. In any event, he did audit the books and found some sort of a discrepancy in the accounting procedure and he immediately closed the post office. That post office is still not open.
It took 23 days to advertise the opening of a position for a new postmaster. I am led to believe it took this long because when it was being advertised the advertisement first had to go to Ottawa to the Postmaster General in case he had someone he wanted to appoint to that job. This caused a delay. People in that community since the closing of that post office have not been receiving their hydro bills through the mail. As a result, many of them had their electric services completely cut off. Many old age pensioners have not received their cheques. They were told by the Post Office Department that mail could be picked up in Winnipeg, but that is 280 air miles away.
The community of Island Lake does not have telephone service, does not have television and there are no roads to the community. The only link the people have with the outside world is by mail. At least when the mail was packed in by a man on snowshoes they were sure of getting mail once a year. Under the present system they are no longer certain of that. Let me also point out the importance and gravity of this situation in respect of those people who are on medication. They depend on receiving this medication by mail. When the mail service was stopped many of these people had to turn to the airlines and have their medication shipped in by air express. This is a costly item for people on old age security. The same is true in respect of eyeglass prescriptions, and so on.
The irony of the situation is that if an accounting discrepancy such as this occurred in a community closer to the hub or the capital of the nation, I do not think the people would stand idly by while the Post Office Department took that sort of action. I do not know what the Post Office is trying to do. It waited for 23 days in this case before advertising for a new postmaster. Obviously, the process takes several months to accomplish. In the meantime, the department says the postmaster or the band of Indians which looked after the mail service had done something wrong so they are being penalized by not having mail service for three months.
Another northern community, Poplar River, which is 300 air miles from Winnipeg, has not had mail service since the end of February. It took the postal department from the end of January until April 6 to advertise for a new post-
Business of Supply
master. The people of this community were told in a letter that they could pick up their mail at Selkirk, which is 300 air miles away. This community also has no roads, no telephones, and so on. How do we expect these communities to operate?
When I post a letter and put an 8-cent stamp on it, or a 12-cent stamp, which will be the case in the future, it seems to me there is a guarantee that the letter will be delivered to the person to whom it is addressed. I have a number of pieces of correspondence from the people in these isolated communites which were sent out by carriers, such as a pilot or somebody who happened to be going out. They have told me they have not even been able to get repairs for some of their small outboard motors because normally the parts are ordered by mail.
The postal department has tied up these communities without any thought whatsoever for the convenience of the people. We are not just talking about 1,200 people in one community, but 400 in another, 300 in another, and right across the country. I cannot see why the postal authorities should be allowed to just walk in and close down a post office because of a discrepancy, without giving the community any opportunity whatsoever of reimbursing the post office for the loss. It has never been proven to me that there was a discrepancy; it has only been mentioned in several letters. The people of these communities are pleading for their postal services back. They are saying that perhaps something wrong was done, but they have been penalized now by a loss of service for a period of 3'/2 to 4 months; they have done their penance and should now have mail service.
The other matter I should like to mention at this time is the manner in which mail is handled throughout the north. It would seem that long-term contracts are handed out to mail couriers. These can become obsolete with the discontinuation of air service and because of a more convenient way to get mail to certain areas of the north. I have written the Post Office inquiring about this but have received no positive response other than that this has been the system for years and cannot be changed.
I would ask that these problems be looked into and that some action be taken on them immediately because, as I said before, this mail service is the vital link for all the north. Without mail service the community is absolutely dead. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, which is responsible for the treaty Indian people in these three communities I mentioned, I do not think really has taken any initiative in going to the Postmaster General to see whether this matter could be straightened out. I hope the Postmaster General is not even aware that this is happening and that it is a nightmare case that can be blamed on the regional or district office.
I do not blame this Postmaster General for not taking action if he did not know the situation existed. I mentioned, in the case of Island Lake, that I did see a piece of correspondence which indicated that the community would receive its mail from another post office eight miles away. To the people down here this distance may not look great, but to the people in the community that eight miles

represents a journey across water, and at breakup in the spring these people are without service for at least six weeks. At other times, if they want to get their mail they have to travel by means of outboard motor a distance of six miles. Also, that is only in respect of first-class mail.
