speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to reply briefly to the hon. member for Churchill with whom I have a great deal of communication because he does very assiduously concern himself with the problem of mail delivery in the north, which is a type of business I do not think private enterprise would want. We have 8,600 post offices in Canada. The people of the north deserve the best possible treatment that can be afforded them. I think philosophically we agree. On the few occasions on which he has brought matters to my attention, I have tried to act on them. I think he will agree that that is so. He said I have the right to name postmasters. It seems that I have missed out after all these years on some patronage, because I have not named a postmaster since I have been Postmaster General. I shall inquire why I was not made aware of my privileges in this regard.
I am aware of the situation at Garden Hill. If we were to defend ourselves adequately, we could cause some harm to people and I prefer not to do that. I might speak generally about this deficit. This particular community is involved in a deficit of $10,000, which is a lot of taxpayers, money, going back to 1973. The arrangement in respect of the choice of Winnipeg as an alternate source of obtaining mail in the interval while the dispute is being settled has virtually been completed. It was not our choice. It was the choice of the band. We had suggested the Hudson Bay post, which is only nine miles away. The hon. gentleman says that this is a long distance in the north. However, they opted for a distance of 300 miles possibly because of a matter of principle or rivalry, although I am not sure what the reason is.
We have an obligation to collect deficits and close the post offices which we think are inefficient. Fraud may not be involved here. It may merely be a lack of carrying out the rules. These deficits are established. The procedure is painful. We tried to find another post office and another postmaster in this area. We have agreed with the representatives of the people affected to establish very early in the week the precise amount we think is owing. We have discussed the matter with the band in great depth and hope to have a meeting very shortly. This matter, which is of particular significance to many Indian people who depend on the mail, I do not think is entirely a problem involving the Post Office. The problem is that we cannot continue the procedure which ran up the deficit which has existed since 1973. This is a deficit in the sense of money owing to the Crown or the taxpayers of Canada which has not been turned over to them. This, basically, is the prob-

lem in this particular area. Our alternative was to use the post office nine miles away, but the band preferred to use Winnipeg. I am aware of the problem. There has been continuing dialogue and discussion over the last few weeks. The matter should be resolved very rapidly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the members of this House know, I am a supporter of the government. I am a proud supporter of the government and in particular of the government's restraint program. However, while I support the restraint program I wish to bring the attention of this House to a decision taken by the Postmaster General which I find unacceptable. I shall ask him if he will reconsider that decision.
My constituency of York Centre in the northern part of Toronto is almost a fully built-up and occupied area. In a rather dense development a street, Blackhawk Way, is being finished on which there will be townhouses and an apartment building. At the moment there are 24 town-houses. By the time the development is completed there will be 129 homes. People have already begun to move in. In fact, there have been people living on the street for a few months. They have been unable to obtain postal service in that area. I wrote the minister about this. It would seem to me that normal postal service should be extended to an area like this inasmuch as the street is completed and people are living there. The minister replied on April 15, telling me that the federal policy of restraint on spending prevented his adding another postman in that particular area.
Surely something can be done about this problem. If the restraint program is to be applied to the Post Office, and I do not disagree with that, it should not be applied in a discriminatory way in respect of the development of new services. The people who live in this postal area are entitled to have their mail delivered in the same way it is delivered to other people in the area. I am told that although there are only 24 new households on this walk, the postmen on either side already have a full schedule of households and that under the union agreement neither of them is permitted to add even these extra 24 homes on the street and which are now occupied.
I would think that between a more equitable application of the controls program and some reasonable discussion with the postmen concerned on either side and with their bargaining representatives, it might be possible to return to doing the job which the Post Office is bound to do, which is to deliver the mail to the people living in that area. I hope that the minister will have some good news for us.
I was particularly disturbed-and I will conclude with that-to see him note in the letter that it would be necessary to wait until the limitations or restraints are removed. This restraint program is in effect for three years. Does that mean that the people on Blackhawk Way in north Toronto will have to wait for three years before they can start to get postal delivery? I would remind the minister that the Post Office, to which they have been invited to walk, is over a mile away from some of the houses on that street.
May 21, 1976

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will be ambivalent here. These cases come up all the time. I am quite pleased that a Liberal member asks me this question because I have been accused of favouring Liberal members. But now we have heard a negative representation from a Liberal.
The fact is that many thousands of Canadians do not have door to door delivery. Here it is a matter of lack of co-operation by the unions. It is the unions which spelled out in the agreement the number of pieces of mail mailmen can be expected to deliver in eight hours. We will have another look at this particular problem presented by the hon. gentleman, but I wish to point out in general that there are limitations on the size of the work force which were not imposed by the Postmaster General but rather by the size of the budget, the restrictions and the directives of the Treasury Board in light of the government restraint policy. This means that there are many Canadians who will be inconvenienced to the point sometimes of having to walk a mile to pick up their mail rather than having it delivered door to door.
The question is whether there should be a restructuring of the routes with the co-operation of the union, or whether by some other method we can implement door to door delivery in the hon. gentleman's riding. We will review this again, but I want the hon. member to know that there are hundreds of such cases across Canada at present and the only way in which we could satisfy every request would be possibly to hire another 50 or 100 letter carriers at a time when we do not have such a mandate. We are trying to accommodate as many people as possible by continually reviewing our route structure and the workload of the postal employees because I do agree that, as a general principle, wherever the population warrants it Canadians should have mail delivery door to door.

Mr. Chairman, I am taking part in these discussions today for many reasons which not only concern myself but Canadians from coast to coast. The primary reason of course is the general inefficiency of the Post Office as a whole, and I am glad to see that even the parliamentary secretaries on the other side are in opposition to the way in which the Post Office is being run.
However, before I begin my remarks, and in fairness to my friend, the Postmaster General, I want to take this opportunity to offer my belated condolences to him for inheriting the department in the mess in which it is in, a mess which probably the Post Office Department has never seen in the history of the mail service. He inherited it from the former minister, the hon. member for Papineau, who will probably go down in history not only as the most incompetent minister but certainly as most untrustworthy, as witnessed by his resignation as minister of consumer and corporate affairs.
Oh, oh!

Because coincidentally the Postmaster General has acquired that portfolio as well from the hon. member for Papineau, I sympathize with him doubly. The only consolation that he can have is that the former minister was not minister of consumer and corporate affairs long enough to bring that department down to the all time low to which he brought the Post Office.	,
Business of Supply
In any case the major concerns regarding the Post Office were ably presented by my colleague, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, who so eloquently brought to light the many inefficiencies and mismanagement in the Post Office. Because of my concern regarding strikes and walkouts, particularly within the Post Office and other essential services, I would like to find out from the minister whether he or indeed the government has any long range suggestions to overcome the labour unrest which plagued us in the past.
We all know that in just five years the Post Office had a total of 24 illegal strikes around the country, causing untold inconveniences and hardships for the public and for industry. They were the cause of many bankruptcies within the segment of our economy which forms the backbone of our industrial life, and I am of course referring to the small businessman who seems to be neglected by large governments, large unions, and large multinational corporations each day. Because of the fact that he is a small businessman he is unable to do very much, if anything, on his own to overcome his problems. Yet this government, and specifically the Post Office Department, deals with these illegal and other strikes on a day by day basis as it does with almost everything, rather than establishing a comprehensive long range program to deal with matters relating to labour unrest mainly in essential services such as that provided by the Post Office. In this regard it is no secret that I, along with the majority of my constituents, would like to see the right to strike taken away from individuals and groups of individuals within areas that adversely affect the well-being of our nation, and of course the starting point could be the Post Office.
There are other general and pertinent questions which must be answered, such as the fact that federal departments, because of their dissatisfaction with the unreliable mail service are now resorting to the use of couriers, and the rising amount of theft and loss within the Post Office. I understand that the Post Office has admitted to a loss of nearly half a million pieces in the last five years alone. This is a disgrace, it is unbelievable.
Another such matter is the unrealistic deficit within the Post Office, the fact that operating expenses have increased by 24.6 per cent, a matter which is hard to comprehend when the same government under which the Post Office Department operates is advocating guidelines and controls to be applied by the rest of the country far below that level. It can be easily said: do unto others as you do unto yourself. But unfortunately this is not the case with the government.
I could go on and on about the mish-mash of inefficiencies and mismanagement within the department, not only under the minister's predecessor but under the minister himself, but, as I said at the outset, my colleagues who spoke before me today and those who will follow me this afternoon will speak in detail on these questions which should and indeed must be answered for the benefit of all Canadians.
I would now like to dwell on a more specific subject which relates to the minister's responsibility with regard to the Olympics. I am of course referring to the Olympic coins, stamps, and medallions so far as production, sales, distribution and, I hope, profits are concerned. I am certain
95 5 68-38'/z

May 21, 1976
Business of Supply
that, unlike the minister's predecessor, the Postmaster General will not in answer to my questions relating to the Olympics bring forth racial discrimination as did his predecessor on every occasion that I brought the matter of the Olympics before the House.
The minister knows very well that I am and always have been very concerned about the way in which the Olympics have been handled so far as the financing and staging of the games is concerned. He knows also that I have attempted to co-operate with the government on this matter to the best of my ability.
However, in this respect let me begin by saying that the result of the coin and stamp programs to date is a far cry from the objective the Post Office set as a goal when the Olympic Act passed through this House two years or so ago. In fact, what had been realized in net profits compared with the original projected forecast by the Post Office is a disgrace. Instead of net profits of $250 million, total sales of Olympic coins as of September 30-sales, not profit-were only $141 million, which is bad enough, but what is worse is that the net profit was less than $35 million, and even now with just months remaining before the program ceases to exist in accordance with the legislation, the forecasts by the coin department indicate that the silver coins alone will contribute $150 million toward the capital cost of the games. That is a nice fat figure, but it is still $100 million less than was originally projected. How can we trust or believe that projection when, out of the seven series, four series realized less than $35 million?
There are only three series to go, and I realize that there are still some coins from the other series yet to be sold, but certainly that $150 million goal at this stage of the game, although it is $100 million behind, is still unrealistic. We simply cannot believe the predictions, based on past performances, and when the minister gets a chance to answer this specific question I would like him to do so.
The minister and the managing director of the program, Mr. Austin Page, boast that no other company or industry in Canada has been as successful as the coin program was under the Postmaster General with regard to net profits. I can only say that no other business has the federal government printing or minting coins in that regard. It is as simple as that. I know the minister will be happy to explain these forecasts. I am sure he will explain why, with all the spending going on, such a concentrated continuation of advertising is taking place in the United States, for example.
I realize that to sell you have to advertise, but it has been proven that in the United States the program has been a disaster. Less than 10 per cent of the total sales have been made in the United States. The advertising program must be very expensive. I will wait for the minister to come up with that figure, but I doubt whether it is worth while at this stage of the game. I think it is really a waste of money.
There are other areas which we cannot understand. What about having to absorb the $1.6 million of the cost in the bank programs within the United States, or the $600,000 advertising costs which have to be absorbed as a result of the Canadian re-solicitation program? I wish the minister-and I know he has difficulty doing this, and I have
[Mr. Jelinek.l
great respect for him, but I am concerned about the programs in his department-on behalf of the program and his department would own up to the fact that there is no doubt in anyone's mind about the inefficient personnel within his department and the Olympic coin program, at least in the area of projections. There has been a total failure in projections, and we cannot continue to believe the projections at this late stage.
I also wish the minister would come clean in this regard, as he often does, and lay the facts on the table as they really are by admitting, unfortunate as it may be, that the coin program has been a big failure, and by producing realistic forecasts which can be trusted, as opposed to past performances. Once that can be counted on we can try to figure out what deficit or what part of the deficit will be able to be absorbed with regard to this coin situation.
Still on the coin side, it would be good to know how many coins are yet to be minted. These are very pertinent questions, and I would like to get the minister's attention now. I know I have been going on at length with regard to the coins, but how many coins are yet to be minted, if any, both in the silver and gold categories? What are the plans for the unsold coins, and is consideration being given to the possibility of continuing the program into 1977? The minister knows that according to the legislation the program will end at the end of this year.
I think the same questions must be answered with regard to the Olympic stamp situation as well, and more than that I understand it to be a fact that there exists a huge surplus of Olympic stamps on hand with little if any possibility of disposing of these stamps on a regular basis. It seems to me that the stamp program is in worse shape than the coin program.
It is hard to believe, but the stamp program has only raised a fraction of the $10 million anticipated by the original projection. Perhaps this is the reason why the Postmaster General saw fit to initiate his own mini lottery within the Post Office. Is the minister not concerned that such contests as the one he has established in the Post Office can result in the use of pressure tactics by wicket clerks, for example, within his department? There are enough problems within the department already without more problems. I say this because since the Post Office has had to resort to such means to sell these stamps, is the minister contemplating the extension of the stamp program into 1977 as well? I hope if this is the case that it will be brought forward in the House in the form of an amendment to the act, and I am quite sure our party would consider that.
However, going back to the mini lottery within the Post Office, perhaps the minister should consider similar contests for regular stamps, and the main prize could be on-time delivery of the winner's mail for one week. That would be something unusual in the Post Office.
The whole question of the Olympic stamp lottery within the Post Office is questionable as to its legitimacy, at least, because it definitely relates to the Olympic legislation passed by parliament-the stamp program-and yet at no time was parliament asked or even advised of this situation. An explanation by the Postmaster General must be given in this regard. The stamp program is tied in with the original Olympic legislation, and therefore nothing which
May 21, 1976

differs from the legislation can be done by the department or by the government unless it comes back before parliament in the form of legislation; I certainly hope there will be some explanation from the minister in this regard.
I would also like an explanation regarding the sale of Olympic stamps to foreign countries at discount prices, which also goes against the Olympic Act. I refer specifically to the United States where these stamps are being sold for less than they are in Canada and then are being bootlegged back into Canada with the profit going to no other than the bootleggers themselves. I realize these schemes are initiated to try to get rid of the stamps, which along with the surplus stamps on hand went unsold, but surely if the minister is going to be changing the legislation which was passed by parliament, parliament should be advised as to any changes within that legislation. Once again, these questions, should and must be answered for the benefit of all involved.
Keep to the right department.

This comes under the Post Office Department, and the Postmaster General knows that very well. The hon. member may not know that, but the minister does.
Last but not least is the Olympic metal stamp sculpture or medallion situation. I am sure the minister will inform us as to the quantities which were ordered, packaged, and sold, and once again, as with the coins and stamps, I am sure he will let us know what the Post Office intends to do with those medallions which cannot be sold, how long this program is intended to continue-the same as with the stamp and coin program-and whether they will go hand in hand or whether it is a separate situation.
You may recall, Mr. Chairman, that Austin Page, the managing director of the coin program, once pooled the Olympic medallion thing with the Olympic coin situation so I assume it can be taken that it falls in the same category.
You may recall, Mr. Chairman, that last October there was a question as to who received the contract to mint and package these medallions and what criteria were used in making the final decision. The reason I bring this matter forward now is because it was my understanding that Mr. Norton Cooper, president of the Jacques Cartier mint, was in fact awarded some if not most of the contracts relating to the medallions, while other reputable Canadian mints whose bids were considerably lower did not receive the consideration they deserved. I say this because the same Mr. Cooper was involved in the past with the prosecution of DREE officials in connection with substantial federal grants that were made to Mr. Cooper's other company, Silver Shield Mines, and it is puzzling to say the least that this individual continues to be favoured by the government of which he illegally took advantage.
It is my understanding that the other well known Canadian mints did not even receive an opportunity to bid on these medallions, and that some contracts regarding the commemorative medals were awarded to a Swiss firm. I am sure that once again the minister would be happy to inform us where these medallions are being produced, by
Business of Supply
whom, and who is responsible for their packaging, distribution, and sale.
As with the other Olympic coins, be they silver or gold, as well as the stamps, we should like to know whether it is the government's intention to extend this program. I think I have already made mention of the problem of unsold products.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to reiterate that from the outset, and along with the majority of my colleagues, I have always been in favour of the Olympic ideal.
Hear, hear!

We have on many occasions criticized the development of the program in regard to financing and in regard to staging. The blame must clearly rest on the shoulders of the federal government which gave to the city of Montreal, to Mayor Drapeau and to COJO, the opportunity to play with matches-and in the process to burn themselves.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I wanted to say, and I am sure that I speak on behalf of many of my colleagues, that I wish the Olympic games the greatest success. I hope that once the Olympic flame dies down we as Canadians can hold our heads up high and be proud that we put on a good Olympics.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I hope the hon. gentleman is not speaking for too many members on the other side. The only greater penalty than a poor service would be to have to read the diatribe that we have had to listen to from the member.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
I would agree that the hon. gentleman is not a racist. We have often discussed that and I think I have protected him against that charge in public. He knows exactly how I feel on that particular subject. It is not an accusation that I would want made against me, so it is not one that I would make lightly. The hon. gentleman need have no fear that, because he is asking questions about the Olympics that are to take place in Quebec, anybody is going to put a racist connotation on his questions. On the other hand, I think if he reads his speech he may find that he has smeared a lot of people himself, and that is not very nice.
We could start with the Olympic stamp sculpture. It was the gentlemen in front of me who issued the contract and I should protect them by pointing out that the Olympic stamp sculptures were tendered by at least three firms in this country. They were not issued to the Jacques Cartier mint. The hon. gentleman, through circumspection, brought in a Mr. Cooper who went bankrupt despite DREE funding four or five years ago, as have thousands of businessmen. The point is that the recent contract was awarded to a large firm in Toronto known as Johnson, Matthey & Mallory Ltd. of Toronto. It is a very responsible organization. I visited the plant and met with the owner, the supervisor of the plant, and the production engineer, to make sure that the metallic sculptures they were producing for us under tender were of a quality to match the first sets that had been made by Jacques Cartier.

May 21, 1976
Business of Supply
The Jacques Cartier mint ran into financial trouble so I felt it should not be included in the subsequent tenders in case it had financial problems again and would not be capable of supplying the merchandize. We took its name off the tender list and issued the contract to Johnson, Matthey & Mallory Ltd. of Toronto. I think it is important that this go on the record.
As an interesting sidelight, Mr. Chairman, that firm had a little trouble with production and the first people they went to for advice was the Jacques Cartier mint.
I do not like smears, Mr. Chairman, and I do not want them on the record even if they are unintentional. These things were tendered, the tender was won by the firm I have mentioned twice. I suspect Johnson, Matthey & Mallory Ltd. is well known in the country. It is a respectable and responsible firm in Toronto and I would imagine it would resent any attack on its integrity, as do my officials.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has asked a lot of basic questions but it was very hard to follow because they were interwoven with a certain amount of bias in philosophy that makes it kind of hard, perhaps, to keep my temper on the matter.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Be nice, Bryce.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
I intend to be nice but it is kind of hard in this situation. I think if the hon. gentleman is sincere he should really start with reading the Debates when the act came into this House and was agreed to by all parties, except the New Democratic Party. It specified what finances were to be placed at the disposal of COJO through the federal government for the building of the Olympics, whether they are held in Montreal, Vancouver or Edmonton is unimportant. That debate is specific and important because the official spokesmen of our party at that time, the President of the Treasury Board, stated that we anticipated raising $100 million from coins. It is in Hansard. I cannot tell the hon. gentleman any more clearly than that. They are not my words. They are not Austin Page's words. They are the words of the hon. minister when he was speaking. He said we would put a ceiling of $250 million on the revenue coming from coins in the event that coins became very popular in the venture.
His own realistic appraisal was that if we were to get $100 million it would be a magnificent effort which we damn well should not be ashamed of as Canadians. I say right now that we will reach that $100 million despite the cynicism of the hon. gentleman opposite, who is not a racist but is without doubt the greatest cynic in the House of Commons.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext: I will also suggest to him-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You are speaking of a former Olympic athlete. Shame on you!
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext: Do you want me to call him an optimist?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley on a point of order.

Mr. Chairman, I have to rise and object to the last statement of the Postmaster General when he called me a cynic. If he wants to call it pessimism he can call it that on the past figures-out of seven coin series four have already been minted and as of last September less than $35 million has been realized. I hope that the Postmaster General withdraws that statement. He may call me a pessimist but not a cynic.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
Maybe I should not call him anything, pessimist or cynic. However, I do not see anything unparliamentary about cynic. If the word cynic bothers the hon. members, I will gladly withdraw it. I hope it is recorded in Hansard that I am withdrawing the word cynic and substituting the word pessimist.
I come back to the hon. member's contribution. I am not reflecting on my predecessor, who is not here to defend himself. He left the Post Office in extraordinary good shape. That extraordinarily good minister is not in the cabinet now because he had the courage to get up and talk to the consumers of this country, and he paid a pretty heavy price for it.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
In case there is any doubt about the integrity of the Mallory firm, they are the ones who prepared the blanks for the Mint. That credential ought to satisfy the hon. member about the quality and integrity of the firm supplying the metallic stamp.
With regard to what will be done with the extras, they will be melted down under the supervision of the Royal Mint or by whatever authority is charged with that. The hon. member should know there will be very few since, basically, we mint them to order. If I am not mistaken, we keep a minimum inventory of metallic stamps on hand.
The important thing about the coin program is that periodically the whole operation is subject to audit by the Auditor General's department. The Auditor General has made an odd footnote where he thinks the operation ought to be tightened up in inventory of samples. There is some question about amounts of money advanced in the United States in the form of advertising. I read the Auditor General's report on the operation several months ago. He gave it a clean bill of health.
On Tuesday next I will be tabling the report. I say to the hon. member that, despite his pessimism, we will hit $100 million which the former President of the Treasury Board said we would hit; not the $250 million that Mayor Drapeau talked about, not the $250 million put in the act in order to make certain that, in the event the coins took off, we did not turn over more. However, we did say in that same speech we would put at the disposal of COJO $375 million from lotteries, stamps and coins. We are not spending here. We are just raising it through three programs. We will meet that, obviously, with the success of the lottery.
Sales through the Olympic coin program amount to over $216 million. Our profit is more than half way to the $100 million. This is one of the reasons why it is being con-
May 21, 1976

tinued. We do not think we will hit the $100 million; we think we will hit $125 million. That should remove some of the pessimism of the hon. member.
On Tuesday next the hon. member will have a copy of this. It contains all the information. I do not want to bore the House now with all the statistics to which they can have access on Tuesday. I simply want to assure him, as a concerned Canadian member of parliament, that the coin program is one Olympic program that will not be stigmatized or have attached to it any kind of scandal. The Auditor General keeps close guard on the operation. The advertising and everything else are properly accounted for. I am satisfied that the operation is being adequately run under Mr. Page.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
