speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
I am not going to get into all the innuendoes of the hon. member. I will simply sum up by saying yes, we will hit $100 million. Yes, we will hit $10 million in stamps. We are over $50 million now. Yes, the surplus metallic stamps will be accounted for and melted down. The metal will be returned to the Royal Mint, or whatever we do, to get a credit. Yes, we are running things in a business-like fashion. Yes, Mr. Page is quite adequate. Yes, we will meet the objective which the President of the Treasury Board set several years ago.
With regard to the matter of the medallions, I do not know anything about that. Our only interest in the medallions is that they do not interfere with the coin program. They are not purchased through the Post Office. To the best of my knowledge they are not purchased through any responsibility of the Postmaster General. I will verify that later, but I am quite certain of it. It is a COJO production. They may or may not have been minted out of the country. I feel certain they were awarded to somebody on tender, but they do not have anything to do with the Postmaster General. If the hon. member wants to say that it does, this is his opportunity, but he had better be accurate. As far as I am concerned, I do not have anything to do with the medallion program and I do not want anything to do with it. I hope the hon. member reflects on the inference he perhaps unintentionally placed on the record. What I have anything to do with, I will stand behind.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to address my remarks on the Post Office to three separate topics. The first two are related and I will cover them together. The last is on a different matter and I will cover it separately. There may be a fourth matter about which I will raise some questions.
Business of Supply
The first matter I would like to bring before the minister is the problem of the lack of communication within the Post Office as to the exact status third-class mail holds. This problem first came to my attention in April of 1976. It seems that the agricultural representative for Huron County sent notices of a meeting to area farmers by third-class mail on April 20. The recipients of the notices did not receive them until as late as April 30 to May 3, a full ten to 12 days after they were originally mailed. As a consequence many of the people involved never got any notice of the meeting until it was over. I believe there was more than one meeting involved.
I was asked to inquire into the problem, and this is when I became aware of the lack of communication on the status of third class mail within the Post Office. The customer service person contacted confirmed that the delay of third class mail is condoned in the Post Office. He did mention, however, that the delay of ten days for delivery of a mailing in a county was unusually long. He also suggested the use of first class postage to assure delivery of notices of the meeting.
It seems evident that in the eyes of the Post Office employees third class mail does not have any status at all. On May 6 I informed the Postmaster General of this problem. I received no answer as to the status of this mail. He suggested I send him complete information and I have since done that. I look forward to the minister making a personal inquiry into the situation as he promised in the House when I raised the question. I believe this will benefit many people who use open envolopes with six cent stamps. They should be made aware of the situation. There is a conflict between Post Office employees and the general public as to the status of third class mail. This presents a serious problem and everyone concerned should be allowed to know what exactly a 6-cent stamp means.
The second matter I should like the Postmaster General to consider is the effect of the proposed increase in the cost of first class mail announced today. The hon. gentleman said there would be an increase of 50 per cent in two stages from the present rate of 8 cents to one of 12 cents. An increase of 50 per cent can hardly be justified during the present time of restraint. If the government plans to increase the rate let us make sure the business community is in agreement. If it is not, business interests might well feel they should turn to the other forms of communication. It would not be surprising if, given the Post Office's record of poor service and inefficiency, the business community were to turn to other forms of communication should they feel this latest increase is unjustified, in which case any additional revenue from the higher postal charges will be more than counterbalanced by a decrease in the total volume of mail carried. The increase announced today could be the beginning of a vicious circle. Finally, let me say that if rates are increased the department must make sure there is a corresponding increase in the quality and efficiency of the service offered to the public.
Another matter I wish to mention is of direct concern to the Department of Public Works, although it clearly comes within the purview of my responsibilities as the spokesman of my party on matters having to do with the Post Office. In the early seventies, as part of the government's

May 21, 1976
Business of Supply
policy to reorganize the Post Office, plans were made for the development of metropolitan area postal plants designed to improve the system of moving mail and to cope with projected future mail volumes. This project was referred to as the MAPP program.
The new MAPP facilities which, for reasons I shall show, are of interest to us today are those in the Toronto area, specifically the large Gateway postal plant at Dixie and Ellington Road, Mississauga, and the downtown Toronto south-central letter processing plant near Lakeshore Boulevard East at Greenwood Avenue. Both these facilities were developed by the Department of Public Works under the project management principle in 1971, and the estimated cost at that time was $80 million. The date of completion was tentatively set for Christmas mail in 1974. This completion date soon proved to be unrealistic. A progress report stated that Gateway would be ready for live mail testing in 1975. The south-central plant was also expected to begin live mail testing some time in 1975. This was the first announcement in a trend which is most revealing and one which, once understood, must be stopped.
The story in its barest form is one of delays and rising costs. As I say, in 1971 the cost was estimated at $80 million, with completion to be effected in December, 1974. In 1975 the facilities were still not completed and the cost was reported to be in the order of $140 million. Today, according to informed sources, the cost is estimated to be in the order of $160 million and it is believed the Toronto plants will not be operative until at least 1977. There is no guarantee that these figures are correct, however, and costs could quite possibly soar to $200 million with a completion date set for 1978.
There is some suspicion that irregularities exist in the terms of the contracts governing these postal plants. They take the form of contracts in which no time limitations are provided, contracts which embody no financial limitations upon contractors or sub-contractors. It is rumoured that the total consultants' bill alone is in the neighbourhood of $20 million. The contractors working on these projects have nothing to lose as long as costs keep increasing and the completion date is extended.
There have been implications, Mr. Chairman, that there is no reason why the buildings should be completed on schedule. There is some suspicion that many interested groups would like to see the projects continue, with further delays and further extra costs. It is felt there was little concern shown for time limitations and cost factors in connection with either of these projects. All this, of course, affects the Post Office and the efficiency with which mail is delivered and, as such, it should be of great concern to the minister responsible for the Post Office. In closing, I should like to ask him three questions: 1. Why have these postal plants suffered such delays and such increases in cost? 2. What will be the final cost of these plants and what are the definite completion dates? 3. What are the terms of the contracts related to the construction of these postal plants that they should allow for such delays and cost increases?
The minister told us today that the Department of Supply and Services looks after equipment and the Department of Public Works looks after buildings. It is surely in the interest of the Post Office Department to make sure

that contracts are awarded in the proper form, and that contractors do the job the Post Office wants them to do.
From my experience in negotiating contracts it is customary in most cases to put in a penalty clause to make sure that the facilities are completed when needed, or by the date contracted for. This is the normal procedure but apparently it was not followed in this instance. The question arises whether these new facilities were necessary in the first place. Perhaps they were not. If they were, is the mail being delayed unduly because they have not been put in place?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext: I shall be very brief, Mr. Chairman, because there are several other members who wish to ask questions. If I should fail to deal with all the point which have been raised I will attempt to do so in my closing remarks. First, let me say that all the hon. member's questions about the new facilities in Toronto are being asked on the wrong estimates. While all these questions may be appropriate, they are being asked in the wrong place. The Minister of Public Works is responsible for the building, for the maintenance, for costs, for services, for architects fees, for consultants fees, and for turning the buildings over to the Post Office. I must confess that I have not come here prepared to answer questions on behalf of his department.

Does the minister not agree that this delay-there appears to have been a delay from the start- affects the Post Office greatly? I would at least ask the minister whether he is making daily representations to the Minister of Public Works and to the Minister of Supply and Services in order to see just what is the hold-up, or does he not need these facilities in the Post Office?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, we need them, and yes, we are not happy with the delay. Perhaps the more fundamental question is, is the delay deliberate? I think the hon. member might be inferring that some people would like to see this work stretched out, and I think that is a pretty strong statement. Perhaps hon. members would like me to help find out, but I am not able to do so because the hon. member who has advanced the question has offered no significant proof that this is the case. I think he would have to be much more precise.
We would like to get into the building as soon as possible. To the best of our knowledge the delays are unintentional. if the hon. gentleman has any information that the delays are intentional, then I think it is his duty as a good Canadian to bring the information forward.

Mr. Chairman, I did try to make it plain. It seems that the terms of the contract allow for this; it is not a question of anyone breaking the law or anything like that. Is the minister able to say anything about the contract itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not seen the contract. I can only repeat that this question is best addressed to the minister in the question period or during the estimates of the Minister of Public Works. I will reply a little later to the question about third class mail, particularly as
May 21, 1976

it affects the organizations and associations in the hon. gentleman's riding.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have enjoyed the debate this afternoon, particularly the remarks of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris whose speech I would describe as the decline and fall of the Post Office. I should like to take a somewhat more optimistic view of the whole scene as I see it, and I think I could probably put a title on my own speech and call it the decline and rise of the Post Office.
On the decline side I have to accept the comments of the minister. We were certainly in serious trouble, and there is no question that we still are. But I see very optimistic signs in the Post Office today and I hope that within the next year or two the situation will change to the point where we can be extremely proud of the Post Office as an institution. There is no question that in the last few years there has been very definite instability in the Post Office. Members on all sides have commented on the number of work stoppages, work to rules and so on, which have made it very difficult for the postal authorities and for the Post Office itself to move mail on schedule. There have been needless delays.
Another problem we have had concerns the employee himself. Traditionally the employee of the Post Office has been someone respected in the community who played a definite role in the community, one who in the past would be equated with a police officer, a fireman, or with people working in other institutions in the community. Over the years I think the postal employee has been downgraded. His role has been diminished, and accordingly his salary has been diminished in relation to these other groups.
Because of this instability to which I have referred we have lost some business that we might otherwise have gained. But there has not been a total loss. As a matter of fact over the last five years there has been an increase in business of 20 per cent, or about one billion pieces of mail distributed by the Post Office annually. Nevertheless there is no doubt that some groups in the community have chosen alternate methods of depatching mail or other goods that would normally be moved by the Post Office. This is one of the major problems that have faced the minister since he took office within the last year and a half.
The Minister told the people of Canada on several occasions during the last year or two that there would be no rate increase of any kind until such time as he saw some improvement in postal service. Today he announced some badly needed rate increases, increases that I understand disturb many members in view of the present period of restraint. Nonetheless these increases are legitimate, even with the anti-inflation program. No part of the anti-inflation program says that price increases cannot be made when they result from cost increases. Certainly the cost increases in the Post Office department far exceed the revenue increases we are seeking.
To return to what I was saying, the minister said he would not increase the rates until he could justify it in terms of better service. I think we are now seeing an improvement in service. Some of our larger customers are
Business of Supply
telling us they are experiencing improvements in service. A period of stability has now come to the Post Office.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What is your question to the minister? Do not waste the time of the committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
This period of stability commenced, I think, with the contract itself. We now have a reasonable contract. Indeed I think it is a good one. Once more the employees are in a position of parity with other groups in the community, and I think this fact alone will increase stability in the Post Office.
Another very important step toward better service and productivity was taken by gradual acceptance of the postal code. We now have an acceptance rate of 57 per cent. Then associated with the code and its acceptance is the whole mechanization program which is fundamentally designed to improve service in the Post Office. This program is only partially completed and some major aspects of it are not yet in play.
Mechanization is partially a fact in Toronto, Hamilton, Vancouver and London. For example, in Toronto two new plants are opening and are now working at 20 to 30 per cent capacity. Toronto, which handles approximately 50 per cent of the mail moved in Canada by the Post Office, is a very key point. We hope that the two plants in Toronto will prove to be very efficient in operation, but it will probably be the end of the year before they are functioning at full efficiency.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: This can only be done with the consent of the hon. member because the time will be taken from his allotted 20 minutes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes, I will, accept a question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: With the improvements the hon. member speaks about in Toronto, where this great bulk of mail is handled, does the hon. member think this will shorten the time it takes to send a letter from Prescott to Ottawa, some 60 miles, which on three occasions last week apparently took seven days? Do you think that automation will help this problem in my constituency?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
I do not think it is going to help that problem, Mr. Chairman, and I never suggested it would. What I am saying is that this one change will help the province. Certainly letters going through Toronto will be facilitated with this new equipment. If the hon. member would just wait for a minute he will hear some of the other solutions I want to suggest.
There is no question in my mind but that one of the major areas of this problem relates to general productivity of the individual and the feeling in the Post Office, or general morale, which is something I think is more important than equipment. I hope to be able to go through all these points in the short time that is available. I agree with the hon. member that this is not a total solution. If the mail is not going through Toronto this equipment certainly is not going to make a difference or solve the problem in that

May 21, 1976
Business of Supply
particular case. However, we will try to satisfy the hon. member in terms of the other points I propose to make.
In addition to this program of mechanization we have a program designed to get more acceptance of the postal code. Incidentally we can expect a very aggressive program fairly shortly, and these plans are under way, designed to increase the use of the code, particularly among the larger business users of the mail service which make up 80 per cent of the postal load. In addition to this move toward greater acceptance of the code we have an aggressive marketing program in terms of using the Post Office and the facilities provided by it. We are particularly concerned about dealing with the larger business users in terms of how they use the mail, how they address their envelopes, how they use the code, the size of their envelopes, and so on.
This aggressive program directed to the business community will be something of which we will see a great deal more in the near future. People will increasingly see the red, white, and blue colours of the Post Office. It is hoped they will become more aware in terms of what the Post Office can do and what the users can do to help get the mail to the point of destination in a limited period of time. There is an aggressiveness which is something we have not had in the Post Office for a very long time, but I think we will see a great deal more of it in the next six months or a year. Even at this stage of the game we are seeing some success. Large and small users, individuals and businesses are suggesting that things are already improving. They are indicating a desire to support the Post Office in its program designed for improved and more efficient service.
The major criticism of the Post Office over the last four or five years has been, and rightfully so, in respect to morale. This is a more difficult problem in the sense that you just cannot buy a machine and turn this thing around, as you can when using the code and mechanization. This is a problem that is associated with people, and I think it is the major problem the Post Office has faced. It is also a major problem facing many industries in this country today. We are talking about the work place itself and the role that the individual has to play.
We are talking about individuals who work 40 of their perhaps 80 waking hours, and the satisfaction those individuals get from their jobs. It is wrong to assume that we in the Post Office and the people who work there are not basically concerned about this problem. I can assure you that there have been meetings recently with senior Post Office officials and employees to discuss this very problem, and how we can improve the service and increase productivity. Bringing management and employees together in the Post Office on a continuing basis is one of the ways we think we can improve the spirit within the Post Office, and eventually the service itself. This has to be brought down to the individual worker. We have to practice industrial democracy, and industrial democracy means giving the workers a share in some of the management decisions in the Post Office.
The other point has to do with the work on the floor of the Post Office and on the postal route. We must make these more meaningful activities and this is something-
How can you do that?
Mr. Chairman, I was wondering if the hon. parliamentary secretary would permit a short question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes.

When the hon. member talks about this involvement in democracy, is he referring to something like participatory democracy? Does he hope this will have the same effect and success that the so-called participatory democracy we heard about at one time enjoyed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the participatory democracy in the terms the hon. member has mentioned is very definitely a current concept, particularly when we see this week that the CLC is talking about participating as a partner with the government, with business and the whole economy.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
I think there is a need for some kind of participation of this kind within the Post Office. These are things we all have to learn something about, including the government. The point of the matter is that we are very concerned about the situation. Another aspect of participatory democracy, as I see it, is the satisfaction an individual gets from his job. This is another area about which we must be concerned. The two have to be brought together so that we do have that kind of participatory democracy.
If the hon. member wants an example, and this is what I think he was leading to, we are talking about a massive marketing program in terms of getting the proper use of the mails by the individual users so that the mail will move quicker and more accurately. We think our employees who are sorting the mail should be dealing with questions of this kind. We think there are roles that can be played by those individuals. We think we can make the work at the Post Office more satisfactory for the individual, and thus make the individual much more productive.
These are some of the problems we are looking at within the Post Office, and I think we are beginning to have some success toward a solution. I must remind hon. members of this aggressive marketing program in fields other than those involving the moving of mail. There is a great deal of criticism about so-called junk mail and so on. There are many areas in which the Post Office should move. We believe we have one of the finest marketing programs in existence in the country, and it is based on the concept that the Post Office Department is the last single entity that drops into almost every household in the country on a daily basis. In some way we are able to move something to the doorstep, the postal box or the point at which our customers receive their mail on a daily basis.
We are trying to find ways to provide a variety of services to the public while at the same time increasing revenue. There has been a continuous growth in mail service, as I mentioned, something like one billion extra pieces per year. It is our belief that this growth will continue. People are going to see the red, white, and blue symbol of the Post Office a great deal more on their television screens, and they are going to see postal employees moving around the community in a strong marketing way. I hope that in a year or so the Post Office in
May 21, 1976

this country will be an institution of which we all can be extremely proud, as a going business.

Mr. Chairman, we have just heard an incredible speech about how the government is going to spend more money, and perhaps increase the deficit. We are going to have the red, white, and blue symbol throughout the community and on the television screen. Since these happen to be the Conservative party's colours I hope this will be borne in mind when the news is being spread.
Let me get down to some specifics about the Post Office generally. I should like to ask the Postmaster General a couple of questions. In small communities people rent postal boxes for which they pay a charge of perhaps $4 or $6 depending on the size of the box. Frequently they ask, since they do not receive the mail at their door, why they should pay the rental fee. They say it is an extra charge and that they are being discriminated against. Each time I inquire of the Postmaster General's department I am told that when there are sufficient people in an area it is cheaper to use letter carriers than to go through the postal box routine. Perhaps the minister could explain it to me a little better.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am taking note of several questions which I will answer all at once. I have noted that and will answer it before the debate is over.

Of course the minister is entitled to follow that procedure. That is one matter with which I wanted to deal.
It has been stated that the department is entering a period of restraint. I do not think most Canadians disagree that there should be restraint. I believe the government should have been in restraint long before it actually got there. However, I am glad to see it is in restraint. One thing, however, concerns me. In going into restraint the postal department has broken its word.
I feel that politicians in general and governments in general are at a fairly low ebb in this country in the sense that people say politicians make promises on which they never deliver and that the government says it will do something but never does. For example, the community of Carleton Place applied for door-to-door service. A survey was made. There are over 2,000 postal drops. On October 7 the Deputy Postmaster General wrote a letter in which he said that I would be pleased to learn that the results of a recently completed survey indicate that Carleton Place now meets the requirements for door-to-door mail delivery and that this service will be established in the next fiscal year. Since the letter stated that the service is to be established in the next fiscal year, which is this year, and since it did not say "might be" or "it is hoped it will be", a commitment has been made.
When a restraint program is in effect I do not believe further commitments should be made. However, once a commitment is made I think it should be honoured otherwise politicians and governments fall into disrepute. The people say that politicians promise things and do not follow through with them. I argued this matter through the mail with the Postmaster General.

How do you get your mail delivered?
Business of Supply

This correspondence took place between October and February, so one can see that it is a lengthy process. The reply I received states:
In my letter of November 4, 1975 I informed you that Carleton Place, Ontario qualified for door-to-door mail delivery and that the service would, in all probability, be established in the summer of 1976.
In the letter the minister talks about an indefinite period and refers to the probability. I want to point out that the promise was "will be established in the fiscal year". The only doubt was in respect of the probability about the summer of 1976.
I can understand the difficulty in respect of the fall or the winter, but I think the promise should be kept. Although I believe the government should follow the restraint program, at the same time I believe it should follow the commitments it has made. During the last election the government promised that in Montreal there would be house-to-house delivery service in the urban community of St. Louis de Terrebonne where there now are 2,550 homes that are without delivery service, in the community of Mascouche where there are some 2,400 homes without delivery service and in Mascouche Heights where there are 2,400 homes without delivery service. If these promises were made prior to a period of restraint I think a government, in order to maintain its credibility and in order to appear to be honest in the eyes of the community, must fulfil its promises. I agree with restraint, but this is sort of attrition in a sense. Sometimes when it is necessary to lay off people it is nicer to do it through attrition because in that way people are a little happier. I should like the Postmaster General to refer to this area as well when he replies.
The Postmaster General made some general remarks concerning the third area about which I should like to inquire. Because of the communications I had had concerning the situation at Carleton Place I contacted the Letter Carriers' Union of Canada. I received a letter from Robert McGarry, the National President, who said that he would discuss the situation and come up with some ideas. Perhaps the best thing I can do is read his letter so that the points he makes will be on the record. He said:
I know for a fact that service could be given to Carleton Place and to the other communities meeting requirements for letter carrier delivery and the Post Office could cut back on the men-years as requested by Treasury Board and still provide this service. The problem is in the refusal to cut back and stop hiring at the executive and top level positions in the Post Office which does little to improve or provide postal service to anybody but provide employment for executive types who cannot make their way in outside industry.
The Post Office was requested to cut back in the increase of staff for next year. The Post Office did all the cutting from the only branch which provides service to the public and that is in the operational category which includes postal clerks, mail service couriers and letter carriers.
The Post Office will increase its total hiring this year by 2.2 per cent, the highest proportionate growth will be at the higher paid executive level which will increase by 9.4 per cent. The technical, administrative support and operational groups which provide the service to the public will increase by 1.8 per cent and it is this kind of planning and thinking that has caused the service to deteriorate to the level we find it at today.
The only business the Post Office should be interested in is delivering mail. The Post Office is top heavy with high priced help which does little or nothing to provide service to the public but in most cases cuts from the service budget to make more money in the budget to hire more high-priced help.

May 21, 1976
Business of Supply
The cost of three of the executive types who will be hired could pay for, if put to proper use, the hiring of the six letter carrier positions necessary to institute delivery into Carleton Place this year.
The answer to the problem in Carleton Place is one which the union has been complaining about for years. The cut back is never in high-priced help but in service personnel such as letter carriers and service to the public.
I would be more than pleased to discuss the method of giving service without increasing the deficit with any group of M.P.'s or with the Postmaster General whom I do meet on occasions.
Since he mentions that he will speak to the Postmaster General about this I think the Postmaster General should take his advice. The final paragraph I wish to quote is as follows:
The make-up of the Post Office to date is 18,000 delivery personnel, 22,000 sortation and mail handling personnel, 20,500 executive and supervisory personnel, which makes one supervisor or executive employee for each two employees who provide the postal service.
If that is a true reflection, then it is a little top heavy with supervisory and executive personnel. I think one supervisor or executive should be able to supervise more than two of the people who do actual door-to-door delivery and other services for the public.
In conclusion I would like to point out that there is a complaint in rural areas about having to pay a fee for those little boxes at local post offices. The Post Office Department always says that it does that because it is more expensive than having letter carriers. In the specific case of Carleton Place where a promise has been made, if it really is cheaper to have letter carriers, I wish they would be used.
Then there are promises for the Montreal suburban areas, and finally there is a reference by Robert McGarry, union national president, talking about the number of people at high levels compared with those doing the marching or the troop work as it refers to Carleton Place. However, in general I thank the Postmaster General.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know what the practice is. I hope to have an opportunity to wind up on an unpartisan note with some pertinent observations about the Post Office. I know there are one or two other hon. members who want to speak, so I will answer very briefly and then at about twenty to five I hope to be given an opportunity.
Bob McGarry, the president of the Letter Carriers' Union, is an excellent president. He has met with me not once but on a dozen occasions. I would be surprised if his philosophy as enunciated in the letter is any other than that all our problems can be solved by adding more letter carriers to the union at the expense of another union's membership. We have terminology whereby supervisors in the Post Office, who are really the bottom line of management, are probably the ones we depend on most to keep the mails going, are probably the most underpaid, and probably the best case for some distribution of our employees' income, which I might be able to have some time to speak about.
If Mr. McGarry wants to reorganize the distribution of the letter carrier workers in such a way that he can provide extra service with the present workers, that is fine. What is really important is that if I told the hon. member

that this summer we would look after his particular problem, then he has my word that that is exactly what will happen. I will review the correspondence, but that commitment is for that particular letter and no other. I have hundreds of requests.
I do not know what Mr. McGarry was referring to, but in 1974 which is, after all, quite a few years ago, our executive strength was 31. If we fill all our positions, and we have not, the executive strength at the end of 1977 will be 34, an increase of only three people. With regard to our scientific and professional group-and there will be more and more and these people coming as the Post Office becomes more and more automated-I think the hon. member knows that the ultimate end of automation is attrition and a shift of the type of characteristics of the people we have to hire for different skills. I will not explain that.
Obviously the hon. member understands industrial relations, but even so, in 1974 there were only 70, and we are contemplating only 93 if we fill all the scientific and professional vacancies in the Post Office.
So Mr. McGarry can make an excellent case for more letter carriers, but he does not have to do so at the expense of somebody else. I think everybody in the Post Office, from the deputy minister to the labourer in the Post Office, is equally important, as long as he does his job, and I will have a chance to talk with Mr. McGarry when he gets back from his holidays. I think he is taking a holiday right now. I hope to talk with him within a month or two. I will discuss with him which executives he thinks I should dispense with and how many letter carriers I can hire in their place.
I think the hon. member asked me about boxes. I will deal with them. The old policy of the lock box rental was at one time pretty well left to the rural areas. Because of problems of restraint and because of continued city growth and urban sprawl, if that is a good word-and we get a lot of that in some parts of the country where new housing developments grow up, which do not necessarily warrant door-to-door mail such as the 2,000 criterion which was mentioned-we have been using boxes and charging about double the price of the rural areas. This is hardly fair in this period of restraint when people have to use this method of obtaining their mail when normally they would have letter carrier service, so what we are doing is reviewing the relationship of the cost of lock box rentals-which, as the hon. gentleman knows, is not an obligation because there are free boxes available in rural areas-between rural and the urban residents, and I imagine that out of that review will probably come a more equitable relationship.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would just like to make a couple of points and ask a couple of questions of the minister in this debate on the estimates of the Post Office Department. First, I want to congratulate the Postmaster General on his many accomplishments in the department. As a man he has some very special and unusual qualities and unusual ability in matters of labour relations.
Thinking back to the strike of last fall, which was perhaps the longest postal strike in Canada's history-I think it was some 41 days-normally with the mail tied up
May 21, 1976

for that period of time one would expect constituents to be irate and writing and complaining, and demanding that the Postmaster General or the government do something. However, in this strike the Postmaster General was able to find an equitable balance between what was fair to the postal workers and what was fair to the Canadian people. From my own constituency I think I received only two letters, one saying "Tell Bryce to hang in there", and the other demanding that the government take action to halt the strike. However, generally the response from at least my constituency, where there are many rural post offices, was that the Postmaster General was making a reasonable and fair proposition in view of all the circumstances which existed in the country at that time relating to the problems of inflation, unemployment, and the implementation of the selective wage and price controls.
In my constituency there are some 42 rural post offices. About 39 of the 42 remained open throughout the strike, and in some areas we were able to have mail service between the small rural post offices on Manitoulin Island. The Postmaster General probably had one of the most difficult times of his political career, but he certainly had the overwhelming support of Canadian people from coast to coast.
There are one or two matters which I would like to bring to the minister's attention. One relates to the provision of a letter carrier walk on the Batchewana Indian reserve, Rankin location, which is located right within the city of Sault Ste. Marie. It contains really only a few streets in a section of the city of Sault Ste. Marie. It has been trying for some time to get a letter carrier walk service there. They have had group boxes at selected places throughout the reserve, and I have made representations on behalf of the chief and band council to have a letter carrier service.
Even though reserves like this are not part of an incorporated city, if they are an integrated section of the street system of a city as this one is, I think they should be treated as part of the city for letter carrier walk service. In this case about 40 homes and public buildings require a letter carrier walk or house-to-house delivery. It only amounts to about 1,000 feet in distance. I should like to see the service implemented on this reserve, Mr. Speaker.
We usually think of Indian reserves as being located in isolated areas but in this case we have a modern subdivision within the city boundaries with sewers, water, a modern industrial park, modern homes, a new band council administrative building, and a new daycare centre is being built which is a credit to the entire band. We should do our best to ensure that a community like this is given postal service equivalent to that of the city which surrounds it. I should like to ask the Postmaster General to look at this again as it has been under consideration by his department for several months.
Another area I should like to mention is the case of the rural route carriers. I think these people are often the unsung heroes of the Post Office Department. They are really contractors, not employees. They do not accumulate a pension and their job is rather insecure as they have to tender for the contract and, of course, the lowest tender wins. In the vast majority of cases, however, the people
Business of Supply
concerned are very dependable and go out regardless of weather, regardless of road conditions. They provide a very important service to people in rural areas-perhaps one of the most important services.
A few years ago the Post Office proposed that the contracts-which I believe run on a statutory basis for some five years-be changed so that there would be a regular indexing of income. The contract involves running a vehicle as well as wages, and it is difficult to pick an index which is completely satisfactory. I think we should try to move toward regular indexing of the contracts, however, especially in days of high inflation such as last summer when the index went over 11 per cent. I am sure we are all very pleased that the anti-inflation program is working so well that it is now below 9 per cent and, as the year goes on, I am sure it will come down to 8 per cent. Even with the 7 per cent or 8 per cent that we will probably see this year we should have some sort of automatic indexing for the rural route contractor.
Another matter to be considered is the automatic retendering of contracts over $10,000 every five years. There is an automatic requirement that it be tendered, otherwise it could be carried on beyond the five year limit.
These proposals have been in the offing with the Department of the Post Office and I would welcome the Postmaster General's views on them. There are a large number of rural route carriers in my constituency and they are very important people to the communities they service.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words concerning the philatelic section of the Post Office. First of all, however, I want to take issue with an answer given earlier by the minister when he was commenting on the eight cents or ten cents it may cost the individual in Canada to send a letter. He said most people would only send half a dozen letters per year. According to the estimates, first class postage revenues will be $400 million, and the increase the minister has announced will therefore cost Canadian taxpayers $200 million. Any way you look at it, the cost will be $10 per person in this country, not ten cents. While that may seem a small amount it is 100 times the figure the minister gave earlier.
He said that 80 per cent of the postage in this country is paid by 20 per cent of the customers. That means that business pays, Mr. Chairman. But who does the minister think pays for the business postage? Of course it is deducted to arrive at the taxable income so 50 per cent of it will directly come off the national revenue. The other 50 per cent will be passed on to customers by business. Again, the taxpayer will pay. Unlike the Post Office, business concerns in this country have to abide by anti-inflation rules. They are allowed to pass on price increases, however. I should like to hear the minister's comments on this point.
The philatelic section of the Post Office is very important, Mr. Speaker. From time to time the minister has sent letters saying he is proud of the various new issues. The fact that the Post Office has a separate section for philatelists shows that this service is regarded as very important. In a letter circulated last Christmas the minister made reference to his severest critics-the philatelists of the country. If it is true that they are his severest critics then I cannot understand why he does not pay attention to them.

May 21, 1976
Business of Supply
An article in the September, 1974 issue of "The Stamp Magazine" begins at page 60:
Not so very long ago Canada was one of the most respectable stampissuing countries, with a long-standing tradition for fine stamps, a moderate stamp issuing policy, and a wealth of fascinating classical material.
The article goes on to explain the drastic changes taking place in the world of philately and challenges the Post Office to publish the sale and cost figures for the various issues that now proliferate. I believe this challenge has been issued before but there has been no response from the minister. The article comments on the number of examples pointing out how a greedy stamp issue policy can damage the image of the country.
I assume that the Post Office believes philately to be an important source of revenue, Mr. Chairman, because those stamps do not require any service. If the Post Office continues with its present policy, however, collectors will just abandon Canadian stamps. It is a very easy thing for a collector to just stop.
As an example of the proliferation, I would point to a release issued by the minister commenting on the 1975 stamp program, in which there were to be 34 issues. Of these, 11, or one-third, were related to the Olympic program and had some significance, but there were still 23 brand new stamp issues available for the collector. Even this month there is a new issue commemorating the centenary of the Royal Miltary College of Canada. I know that time is limited. Some of my colleagues have a few words to say. However, I hope the minister will make some sort of response.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for bringing to my attention and that of the committee another very important segment of the Post Office, that of the philatelic world. I agree that I said they are the greatest critics. They are also our most constructive critics. We meet very often with representatives of the magazine industry who are dedicated to this particular group of Canadians and, in fact, people around the world who save stamps.
Naturally some collectors complain about the quality, number of issues, and number of stamps in an issue. It affects the value of the stamps, especially if you are interested in speculation. However, I am rather surprised the hon. member would object to the issue of a stamp honouring the Royal Military College.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is not the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
The point is that we get thousands of requests from all members of the House. The hon. member opposite is no exception. We honour the one hundredth anniversary of this or that group or this or that community. As the country gets older, we get more and more of these requests. We are asked to honour this or that event or patent. It is difficult to keep down the number of issues.
I was heavily criticized in the philatelic world for issuing a stamp honouring the Calgary Stampede. It is uniquely Canadian and I thought it deserved honour. Nevertheless, it resulted in a lot of criticism. On balance, I expect this. It is the type of field we are in.

We are asked why Calgary, not Edmonton, or why Edmonton and not another community; why a stamp for the Caisse Populaire or the gentleman who first brought into being credit unions in this country.
We have an advisory group of Canadian citizens. They determine out of all these requests what is the most appropriate design. I get as far away from it as I can for the simple reason these are people who understand the business. They are artists such as Peter Swan. They include representatives of those who produce the stamp, either by offset or letterpress.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I regret having to interrupt the minister, but pursuant to Standing Order 58(9)(a) and (9)(c) I have to put the question at this time.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Carry on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There seems to be some disposition to carry on until five o'clock.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is saying, as he did last evening, carry on. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka wants to raise some matters with the minister. I wonder if the minister might consider that and answer the questions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Some hon. members are concerned about the possibility of a vote beginning at five o'clock. Is it agreed by unanimous consent that the debate carry on and, at five o'clock, the resolution be accepted and reported to the House?
Agreed.

Mr. Chairman, those who participated in the debate today had parochial questions to ask, and rightly so. The Postmaster General listened to them most sympathetically. I commend him because any time I have had to contact him he has been most cooperative.
I wish to bring a matter to the attention of the Postmaster General that is not parochial. It will cause a great deal of concern to many people. It is suggested that the department is going to do away with stamping envelopes with the name of the town, village or city, and replace that with a number. I wonder whether that is accurate. That is one of the most unpopular things the Post Office Department could do. I do not know what damned idiot dreamed it up. I wish to state in no uncertain terms that I am against it. I have before me two cancelled stamps. On one, the cancellation reads;
Postes Canada Post

That indicates where the letter came from.
Is that Parry Sound?

No, that is Scarborough. However, who in hell living in Scarborough would know that? Here is another example:
Postes Canada Post

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
stagedirection
speechtext:
That is the great western city of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. I have a similar stamp from the United States where I believe the same program was being carried out. However, I am informed that all hell broke loose in that country and they have since changed their ideas.
If the Canadian Post Office has any such idea in mind, it will be bombarded with letters from one end of the country to the other. If the minister thinks there was a lot of mail on the capital punishment or the gun control issue, I will tell him there will be ten times as many with regard to this. The minister should tell the official who dreamed this up that if he wants to keep his job, he will scrap this idea right away.
There is another matter. It may seem rather parochial, but it is not. I speak on behalf of the Canadian weekly newspapers. I know that the Postmaster General is sympathetic. These newspapers serve the rural people of Canada. The Canadian Periodical Publishers' Association has asked the czar of the Anti-Inflation Board to roll back proposed postal increases. I quote from their publication:
CPPA and the Canadian Community Newspapers Association joined in making a formal application to the Anti-Inflation Board for a rollback in the new international postal rates for second class mail. Effective January 1, rates jumped from 5 cents a copy to 20 cents and from 7 cents to 36 cents for magazines mailed to the U.S. weighing four ounces and eight ounces respectively. The Post Office omitted notifying publishers despite a steady stream of correspondence on other postal matters such as coding and pre-sorting requirements.
I hope the Postmaster General will look into this. I am aware there may be some increase in rates to the Canadian weekly newspapers, possibly 20 per cent. In all fairness, the Postmaster General said he will reconsider this. I certainly hope that he will. The weekly newspaper is one of the greatest assets to the country, and especially to the rural country.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was about to give the hon. gentleman from Parry Sound-Muskoka some credit. His competence and persistence in making representations on behalf of certain weekly newspapers have resulted in my decision not to include them in the domestic increase I announced today.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
speechtext:
In so far as international rates are concerned, I think hon. members will all appreciate what we had to do, which was to take into consideration the volume of mail coming in from the United States which was subsidized by Canada, against the volume of Canadian periodicals and newspapers going to the United States and which are subsidized by the Americans. There was a great imbalance and both countries agreed to raise their own domestic rates on magazines and newspapers being sent out of the country. This, on balance, was to the benefit of the Canadian newspaper industry.
In the seven minutes left to me I should like to touch briefly on a few subjects-I shall not be able to do any of them justice in that short time. I want to say I think these will probably be my last estimates as Postmaster General. Maybe not. In any event, I want to say that as much as I love the Post Office, I take no credit for it. If I had to make
Business of Supply
an appeal to the Canadian public I would say: This is your Post Office, please listen to one or two of the statistics.
Of all the five departments I have been with there is none I have enjoyed better. It is very people-oriented. There are 52,000 people working in the Post Office, most of them career people. The gentlemen you see sitting here in front of me are not civil servants who spend their time jumping from one department to another. They joined the Post Office 20 or 30 years ago, I suspect from Scotland, most of them; they have a pipeline both into the union and to management that I have never been able to figure out, but it is there. For every Davidson on the union side there is a Sinclair on the management side.
The important thing to remember is that in this country mail is very dependent on factors outside our control. We have six time zones, and climatic conditions play a big role. The lack of an adequate train service hurts us badly. We are very dependent on air mails, and a storm in Toronto, Montreal or Halifax affects mail right across the country, whether we like it or not. Nevertheless by international standards we are considered the third best Post Office in the world.
We are moving five billion pieces of mail in a year. That breaks down the daily potential of complaints to around 200,000. It is very easy, with 200,000 potential complaints, to ridicule the Post Office-not postmasters-they come and go-but the Post Office. One newspaper carried headlines "Body Lost in the Mail". It was great. It was fun; but not so funny for the workers, you know. When you got into it you found they were speaking about the remains of a body. The story began to change a little. They were talking about the cremated remains being sent to a dearly beloved who was 40 miles away and could not attend the cremation. They were being sent by an undertaker who could not find 75 cents to insure or register the packet. It was a little thought-provoking. Where is our sense of values?
It is not my Post Office, it is our Post Office. We have an obligation to make sure that it is improved. What about the deficit? The deficit sounds very high, and it is high. We must, however, take into consideration depreciation and the rent of public buildings which is growing as we move into these new large premises. We also have to take into consideration depreciation on the new machinery which is coming on stream.
Our work force is highly paid, now; our men are adequately paid, they have complete job security, nobody is affected by automation, nobody will be laid off. The rates for working on new equipment have all been firmly established. I do not think there are many in private industry who have the benefit of collective agreements such as the postal unions enjoy. In fairness to the unions, they have withdrawn the boycott of the postal code, and as we increase the use of the postal code we increase tremendously the efficiency of the Post Office.
The rather stodgy image of the Post Office was the first thing which surprised me when I took over, because it is so unrealistic. The Post Office marketing division is aggressive. We have brought in marketing people from the outside. We notice this in the Post Office. We go out to get the business. When I mentioned that 80 per cent of the mail comes from 20 per cent of our customers, I was referring to the business community. I was not talking about the

May 21, 1976
Business of Supply
individual letters which people write and which go first class. The hon. member rightly said that the cost of mailing, in the case of the business community, is passed on to the consumer eventually. So is the postal deficit. Whatever way you want to look at it, I won't argue.
The important thing is that the Post Office is on the road to recovery as indicated by the performance charts which the department keeps, not me. It is indicated by the growing volume of mail, it is indicated by the growing volume of mail, it is indicated by our relationship with industry, particularly the direct mail industry, which is probably the largest employer of help in this country. Though I do not like the term junk mail, we have a very close relationship with them. The new rates were discussed with them in depth. As so many speakers correctly said, the point they were most concerned about was not the higher charge but how reliable are the mails. We can improve in that area. The workers must understand, however, that if the Post Office becomes more inefficient it is their jobs which will go, not mine. They have a stake in the future of the Post Office.
Talking about industrial democracy, I think the hon. gentleman made one very valid point. The letter carriers have incentives in this free entreprise system. When they finish their bag of mail, one which has been measured scientifically, one which has been the study of time studies and methodology, they can go home. When they have done, after a period of six hours, seven hours or five hours, they can go home. The inside worker needs the same type of incentive. He does not have it.
What we need inside the Post Office is job measurement so that we can share with the worker by way of a shorter work week the increase in productivity which the new equipment makes possible. In order to do this we need a
measurement device which both management and labour think is fair. The increase beyond a certain point should be shared in some tangible manner with the postal worker. Then we could get productivity out of what I believe to be a wonderful group of people, those who work in the Post Office.
